question: भारतीय संविधान में 'Basic Structure Doctrine' (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) का स्वास्थ्य नीति निर्माण पर क्या प्रभाव पड़ा है और 'Right to Health' को basic structure का हिस्सा मानने के क्या तर्क और प्रति-तर्क हैं?

options.text: Basic Structure Doctrine — स्वास्थ्य नीति से सर्वथा असंबंधित है

Kesavananda: Parliament unlimited amendment नहीं कर सकता; 'Right to Life' (Art. 21) basic structure है → Right to Health इसका अनिवार्य हिस्सा; लेकिन explicit constitutional right to health absent — DPSP (Art. 47) non-justiciable tension
Basic Structure Doctrine — DPSP को Fundamental Rights से ऊपर रखता है
Right to Health — 1976 में 42वें संशोधन द्वारा basic structure में जोड़ा गया

explanation: Basic Structure Doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973): Parliament cannot amend constitutional provisions that destroy basic structure. Art. 21 (Right to Life) → SC expanded to include Right to Health (Paschim Banga, 1996; Vincent Panikurlangara, 1987). Arguments for Right to Health as basic structure: (1) Without health, dignity/liberty meaningless, (2) Art. 21 = 'life with dignity,' (3) Universal Declaration + ICESCR Art. 12. Counter-arguments: (1) DPSP Art. 47 deliberately non-justiciable (Constituent Assembly decision), (2) Resource allocation = executive/legislative domain (separation of powers), (3) No explicit constitutional text. Current status: Right to Health = implied in Art. 21 (SC interpretation), but no standalone fundamental right. Rajasthan RTH Act 2023 = state-level statutory right. Implication for HEO: health programs cannot be arbitrarily discontinued — constitutional anchor।

question: भारत में 'Cooperative Federalism' बनाम 'Competitive Federalism' की tension को NITI Aayog Health Index और 15th Finance Commission के conditional grants के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: Cooperative और Competitive Federalism — Indian context में identical हैं

NITI Health Index (competitive — states ranked, top rewarded) vs. FC conditional grants (cooperative — states must meet spending conditionality for funds) — दोनों mechanisms अलग incentives create करते हैं; tension: autonomy vs accountability vs equity across states
Competitive Federalism — states के बीच race to bottom in health spending है
Cooperative Federalism — ISC (Inter-State Council) द्वारा ही achieve होता है

explanation: Federalism tension in Indian health governance: Cooperative Federalism (working together): 15th FC conditional grants — states get health grants IF they increase health spending to 8% of state budget. NHM PIP process — Centre-State negotiation. ISC health agenda. Competitive Federalism (states competing): NITI Aayog Health Index — ranked annually, best performers get performance grants, naming and shaming poor performers. Critique: (1) Competition may disadvantage low-income states (Bihar, UP — lower baseline, less capacity), (2) Conditional grants may be paternalistic — states know local context better, (3) But competition → innovation (Kerala, Tamil Nadu models). Equity concern: 'Matthew Effect' — better-performing states get more resources. Granville Austin's vision: cooperative federalism — states as partners, not competitors. HEO must navigate Centre-State dynamics in district health planning।

question: 'Separation of Powers' के सिद्धांत की भारतीय संदर्भ में re-examination करें — विशेष रूप से health emergency (COVID-19) में Executive का judicial और legislative oversight को bypass करना।

options.text: India में Separation of Powers — USA जैसी strict है

India: 'functional overlap' model — COVID में NDMA Section 10 + DM Act delegated legislation से executive dominance; Parliament suspended; courts deferential initially; 'collaborative functionalism' का real test
COVID में Supreme Court ने executive को completely restrict किया
Separation of Powers — constitutional provision नहीं, केवल convention है

explanation: Separation of Powers in India — Health Emergency analysis: India's model: 'functional overlapping' not strict separation (Constituent Assembly Debate). COVID-19 stress test: (1) NDMA 2005 Section 10 — National Disaster Management Authority guidelines bypassed Parliament; lockdown guidelines issued as executive orders, (2) Parliament: Budget Session 2020 curtailed, no full monsoon session — executive legislation through ordinances (Banking ordinance, FCRA amendment), (3) Supreme Court: initial deference — 'trust executive' in national emergency (March-April 2020); later activism: oxygen shortage, vaccine pricing (May-June 2021), (4) High Courts: Allahabad, Bombay, Delhi — filled oversight gap on oxygen/hospital issues. Doctrine: 'Collaborative functionalism' (Upendra Baxi) — all three branches work together, not just check each other. HEO: understands that health emergencies involve all three constitutional organs।

question: भारत में 'Judicial Activism' और 'Judicial Overreach' के बीच रेखा कहाँ खिंचती है — PIL-based health rights enforcement और 'polycentricity' problem के संदर्भ में?

options.text: Judicial Activism हमेशा beneficial है और overreach कभी नहीं होता

PIL health victories (right to emergency care, drug pricing) — activism; courts directing specific hospital infrastructure, drug lists = overreach risk; 'polycentric problems' — resource allocation needs democratic, not judicial, decision-making
Supreme Court — health policy में कोई role नहीं होना चाहिए
PIL — High Court में file नहीं हो सकती, केवल SC में

explanation: Judicial Activism vs. Overreach in health: Activism (legitimate): (1) Paschim Banga (1996) — emergency care right, (2) Consumer Education v. Union — right to drug information, (3) Novartis v. Union (Section 3(d) patent) — public health over TRIPS, (4) NALSA v. Union — transgender health rights. Overreach risk: (1) Courts ordering specific drug procurement (bypasses procurement expertise), (2) Infrastructure directions without budget assessment, (3) 'Polycentric problems' (Lon Fuller) — many interdependent variables → courts see only litigant's view, miss systemic trade-offs, (4) Separation of powers: democratic accountability requires Parliament/executive to allocate scarce health resources. Debate: Upendra Baxi — PIL transformed rights; Pratap Bhanu Mehta — PIL became instrument of elite interests. Balance: Courts interpret rights + set standards; implementation = executive domain。

question: Art. 21 के 'Right to Life' के व्याख्यात्मक विस्तार और 'Right to Health' की justiciability की सीमाओं को ICESCR, General Comment 14 के reference में critically analyze करें।

options.text: ICESCR में Right to Health — भारत पर binding नहीं है

Art. 21 expansive interpretation (Maneka, Francis Coralie, Olga Tellis) → health rights emerge; ICESCR Art. 12 (right to highest attainable health) — India ratified 1979; GC 14: 'availability, accessibility, acceptability, quality' — domestically non-justiciable but interpretive tool
ICESCR General Comment 14 — भारत ने adopt किया है इसलिए justiciable है
Right to Health — केवल negative right है (state shall not harm)

explanation: Art. 21 and Right to Health — jurisprudential evolution: (1) Maneka Gandhi v. Union (1978) — 'procedure established by law' must be 'fair, just, reasonable'; Art. 21 = substantive right, (2) Francis Coralie v. UT of Delhi (1981) — 'right to live with human dignity' includes basic necessities, (3) Olga Tellis v. Bombay MC (1985) — livelihood = part of life, (4) Consumer Education — right to generic drug names, (5) Paschim Banga — emergency care. ICESCR Art. 12: India ratified (1979); General Comment 14 (2000) — AAAQ framework (Availability, Accessibility, Acceptability, Quality). Non-justiciability in India: ICESCR = treaty obligation, not domestic law; Parliament must enact legislation. But SC uses GC 14 as interpretive guide (Vishaka v. Rajasthan pattern). Limits: progressive realization principle — state capacity defense. Positive vs. negative rights distinction increasingly blurred in Indian jurisprudence।

question: भारत में 'Delegated Legislation' की health sector में role और इसकी संसदीय oversight की inadequacy को critically evaluate करें — Schedule H, H1, X drugs और NDMA guidelines example से।

options.text: Delegated Legislation — भारत में unconstitutional है

Delegated legislation essential लेकिन problematic: Parliament technical health details नहीं handle कर सकता; लेकिन drug schedules, NDMA lockdown orders — बिना adequate parliamentary scrutiny; Sub-delegation + excessive delegation risks
Drug schedules — Parliament directly तय करती है
Delegated legislation — courts द्वारा review नहीं हो सकती

explanation: Delegated Legislation in Health: Necessity: Parliament cannot micro-manage technical health details (drug approvals, epidemic protocols). Examples: (1) Drugs & Cosmetics Act 1940 → Schedule H, H1, X determined by rules under DCR 1945 → CDSCO recommends → DGHS notifies — Parliament not involved, (2) NDMA Act 2005 → Section 10 → NDMA Guidelines → lockdown orders (COVID) — no Parliament vote, (3) Essential Commodities Act → Drugs Price Control Order — MoC&I notification. Problems: (1) Henry VIII clauses — delegates power to amend parent Act itself, (2) Sub-delegation: CDSCO delegates to state controllers, (3) Parliamentary scrutiny weak — Departmental Standing Committees overwhelmed, (4) Judicial review: ultra vires challenge possible (In Re: Gujarat Electricity case). Good practice: (1) Sunset clauses, (2) Negative/Affirmative resolution procedures, (3) Regulatory impact assessment. HEO: understands which health rules come from Parliament vs. delegated authority।

question: भारत में 'Fiscal Federalism' की health implications को critically analyze करें — vertical fiscal imbalance, grant conditionality, और 'finance follows function' principle के tension।

options.text: Fiscal Federalism — health expenditure से असंबंधित है

Vertical Imbalance: States have health responsibility (State List) but limited own revenue; CSS conditionality distorts state priorities; Finance Commission devolution unconditional but small for health; 'Finance follows function' violated — health functions devolved to PRIs/ULBs without funds
State governments — Central government से अधिक tax revenue collect करते हैं
Centrally Sponsored Schemes — State autonomy को बढ़ाते हैं

explanation: Fiscal Federalism and Health — critical analysis: Vertical Fiscal Imbalance: Center collects ~65% of tax revenue; States have most social sector responsibilities (health, education = State List). Gap filled by: (1) Tax devolution (41% to states — 15th FC), (2) Grants-in-aid (Art. 275), (3) CSS (NHM — 60:40 centre:state ratio). Problems: (1) CSS conditionality: states must spend on Centre-designed programs — distorts state priorities (Tamil Nadu resisted centralized programs), (2) 'Tied hands': 60% of NHM state health budget = CSS, leaving little for state-specific needs, (3) 'Finance follows function' principle (Sarkaria Commission): when 73rd/74th amendments devolved health functions to PRIs/ULBs, funds + functionaries NOT transferred, (4) State capacity variation: Kerala can implement; Jharkhand struggles. Rangarajan formula, Gadgil formula debates. Reform needed: untied funds + genuine 3F devolution।

question: 'Article 356 (President's Rule)' के उपयोग और स्वास्थ्य कार्यक्रमों की continuity पर पड़ने वाले प्रभाव को S.R. Bommai (1994) के बाद critically analyze करें।

options.text: President's Rule में health programs automatically continue होते हैं

Bommai post-1994: Art. 356 का दुरुपयोग कम हुआ; लेकिन जब लागू हो — elected state government replaced by Governor's administration → NHM PIPs delayed, PRI health committees dysfunctional, community governance disrupted
Art. 356 — केवल law and order के लिए, health पर कोई impact नहीं
S.R. Bommai ने Art. 356 को completely eliminate किया

explanation: Art. 356 and health programs: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): SC held Art. 356 subject to judicial review; President's proclamation must be proved on floor of Parliament; 'floor test' required. Effect: Art. 356 invocations reduced (from 90+ times to rare post-1994). When President's Rule imposed — health impact: (1) Elected state government removed → Governor's administration + Central advisors, (2) NHM PIP approval process disrupted — Centre-State negotiation requires elected state government, (3) RKS (Rogi Kalyan Samiti) — hospital management societies lose political accountability, (4) VHSNC linkage to gram panchayat broken if elections suspended, (5) State health budget implementation delayed, (6) ASHA training programs — state-specific adaptations paused. Historical examples: J&K President's Rule (2018-19) — NRHM implementation continuity challenge. HEO must understand political continuity's importance for health program sustainability।

question: भारत में 'Public-Private Partnership (PPP) in Health' के regulatory governance failures को critically examine करें — information asymmetry, market failure और regulatory capture के संदर्भ में।

options.text: PPP in health — सदैव effective होता है और regulation की जरूरत नहीं

Health PPP failures: information asymmetry (patients vs. providers), market failure (public goods, externalities), regulatory capture (CDSCO-pharma, IMA-regulation), moral hazard (PM-JAY fraud), adverse selection (insurance) — justify government role but regulatory state weak
PPP failures — केवल developing countries की समस्या है
Information asymmetry — health market में solve हो गई है (internet से)

explanation: PPP in Health — regulatory governance failures: Market Failures in Health (Arrow, 1963): (1) Information asymmetry: patient doesn't know quality/necessity (physician-induced demand), (2) Public goods: infectious disease control (non-rival, non-excludable), (3) Externalities: vaccination, sanitation, (4) Uncertainty + insurance market failures (adverse selection, moral hazard). PPP-specific problems: (1) PM-JAY fraud: package manipulation, ghost beneficiaries, unnecessary procedures, (2) Dialysis PPP (NHM): quality complaints, (3) Diagnostic PPP: over-testing, (4) CDSCO: 'regulatory capture' — industry funds drug approvals, revolving door (officials join pharma post-retirement), (5) Clinical Establishments Act — voluntary state adoption; weak enforcement. Remedies: (1) Social Health Insurance with strong regulation, (2) Clinical audits, (3) Grievance redressal (CGRA), (4) Transparency (clinical outcomes data public), (5) Empowered independent regulator (like IRDA for insurance)。

question: भारत में 'Judicial Review of Health Policy' की limitations को Marbury v. Madison tradition और Indian constitutional context में critically analyze करें — 'political question doctrine' और health resource allocation।

options.text: Judicial Review — health resource allocation को fully control करता है

India में political question doctrine — limited but evolving; SC avoided direct resource allocation (Sodan Singh v. NDMC) but intervened selectively (COVID oxygen, vaccine pricing); 'reasonableness review' vs. 'proportionality review' debate — health rights enforcement needs principled approach
Marbury v. Madison — India पर applicable है
Health budget allocation — Courts द्वारा decided होना चाहिए

explanation: Judicial Review of Health Policy — limitations: Political Question Doctrine (USA): Courts avoid 'purely political questions' (Baker v. Carr criteria). India: SC has no explicit political question doctrine but practices restraint in budget/policy. Health cases: Avoided: (1) Sodan Singh — SC avoided prescribing specific health budget %, (2) Mohini Jain — education fee regulation (SC overruled later), (3) Post-COVID vaccine pricing: SC 'noted' government's response but didn't prescribe price. Intervened: (1) Oxygen crisis (2021): SC appointed National Task Force, (2) Essential medicines: some direction on availability. Proportionality Review (emerging): German model — law must be (1) legitimate aim, (2) necessary, (3) proportionate. Indian SC increasingly uses proportionality in fundamental rights cases (KS Puttaswamy privacy case). Health implications: Government must show health budget cuts are 'proportionate' — not arbitrary. HEO: understands courts are backstop, not first-line health planners।

question: Sarkaria Commission (1983) और Punchhi Commission (2007) की संघीय health governance recommendations को critically compare करें — क्या subsequent governments ने implement किया?

options.text: Sarkaria Commission ने health को specifically address नहीं किया

Sarkaria: CSS proliferation reduce करो, states को more autonomy; ISC activate करो; Punchhi: Concurrent List health reform, Governor's role curtail, regional councils. Implementation: partial — CSS reform (NHM rationalization 2014) लेकिन centralization tendency remains
Punchhi Commission की सभी recommendations implement हो गईं
दोनों Commissions — केवल Centre-State financial relations को address करते हैं

explanation: Sarkaria Commission (1983) — health relevant recommendations: (1) Reduce CSS proliferation — states drowning in central schemes, (2) ISC (Art. 263) — activate for Centre-State coordination including health, (3) Governor should not be partisan — affects state health policymaking continuity. Punchhi Commission (2007): (1) Health in Concurrent List — need consultative mechanism, (2) Regional Councils for health coordination (not implemented), (3) CSS reform — states should have more say in design, (4) Governor appointment reform. Implementation record: Partially implemented: (1) CSS rationalization (2014-15): NHM absorbed many schemes (but new ones created — PM-JAY, PM-ABHIM separately), (2) ISC revived (2016 meeting after 10+ years), (3) NITI replaced Planning Commission — states in Governing Council. Not implemented: Concurrent List consultation mechanism, Regional Councils, Governor appointment reform. GAP: Still no legally binding Centre-State health consultation forum।

question: 'Emergency Provisions' (Arts. 352, 356, 360) के under health rights की justiciability और 'suspended animation' of fundamental rights को critically examine करें — COVID और ADM Jabalpur overruling।

options.text: National Emergency में सभी health rights suspend हो जाते हैं

ADM Jabalpur (1976) — Emergency में Art. 21 suspended; overruled in KS Puttaswamy (2017); post-Puttaswamy: even in National Emergency, core of Art. 21 (including Right to Health) cannot be suspended — dignity is inalienable
COVID was declared National Emergency under Art. 352
Art. 359 — Fundamental Rights को Emergency में automatically suspend करता है

explanation: Emergency and Health Rights: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976): SC 4:1 held during Emergency (Art. 359 suspension of Art. 21) — no habeas corpus; Justice Khanna's dissent: 'Even President cannot deprive of life without legal authority.' Overruled: KS Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — unanimously overruled ADM Jabalpur; Right to Privacy + Dignity = core of Art. 21; cannot be suspended even during Emergency. Post-Puttaswamy health implications: (1) Health rights = core of Art. 21 dignity → even National Emergency cannot eliminate right to emergency medical care, (2) Government must provide minimum core health rights regardless of emergency, (3) COVID (2020): NOT declared National Emergency (Art. 352) — NDMA Act used instead; allowed maintaining judicial oversight, (4) Art. 360 (Financial Emergency): never declared — if declared, health spending could face cuts but Art. 21 core must survive. HEO: health rights have constitutional floor even in crises。

question: भारत में 'Inter-State Water Disputes' (Art. 262) और उनके public health implications को critically analyze करें — Cauvery, Krishna, Mahanadi conflicts और health-water nexus।

options.text: Water disputes — public health से असंबंधित हैं

Art. 262 bars SC jurisdiction on water disputes; Tribunals (CWDT, KWT, BDWDT) take decades; water scarcity → diarrheal disease, malnutrition, fluorosis, arsenic; 'Water-Health' nexus in health planning neglected at inter-state level
Supreme Court — inter-state water disputes directly decide करती है
Water — Concurrent List में है

explanation: Inter-State Water Disputes and Health: Constitutional provision: Art. 262 — Parliament may provide for adjudication; SC jurisdiction excluded (ISWD Act 1956 excludes SC). Tribunals: Cauvery (CWDT 1990, award 2007, final 2018); Krishna (KWDT I & II); Mahanadi (MWDT 2018). Health impacts of water disputes: (1) Drinking water scarcity → cholera, typhoid, dysentery epidemics (lower riparian states), (2) Reduced irrigation → malnutrition, (3) Groundwater overexploitation (compensation for surface water loss) → fluorosis (Rajasthan), arsenic toxicity (West Bengal, UP), nitrate contamination, (4) Hydropower conflicts → submergence of tribal health infrastructure. Health planning gap: State health departments rarely represented in water tribunal proceedings; 'Water-Health' nexus absent from ISWD Act. Reform needed: Health impact assessment in water dispute adjudication. Jal Shakti + MoHFW coordination needed but weak。

question: भारत में 'Transformative Constitutionalism' की concept और health rights के progressive realization को Karl Klare's framework और Indian SC's interpretive methodology से critically evaluate करें।

options.text: Transformative Constitutionalism — केवल South African concept है, India में irrelevant

Klare's Transformative Constitutionalism: constitution as agent of social change; Indian SC = transformative in health (Art. 21 expansion, NALSA, Navtej Singh Johar) + regressive (ADM Jabalpur, property rights pre-44th amendment); health rights partially transformative — DPSP gap remains
Indian Constitution — explicitly socialist constitution है, इसलिए health rights fully enforceable
Art. 21 expansion — judicial overreach है, transformative नहीं

explanation: Transformative Constitutionalism and Health Rights: Karl Klare (1998) — 'post-liberal' constitutionalism: constitution designed to transform unjust social structures. Indian Constitution as transformative instrument: (1) Ambedkar's vision: Constitution as instrument of socio-economic transformation, (2) Art. 17 (Untouchability abolition), Art. 46 (Scheduled Castes/Tribes protection), (3) DPSP as socio-economic transformation mandate. SC's transformative moments in health: (1) NALSA v. Union (2014) — transgender rights + health, (2) Navtej Singh Johar (2018) — LGBTQ+ health rights, (3) Paschim Banga — emergency care, (4) Devika Biswas — reproductive rights. SC's regressive moments: (1) ADM Jabalpur (overruled), (2) Pre-Kesavananda property rights priority. Health rights gap: DPSP deliberately non-justiciable (constituent assembly compromise) — limits transformation. Progressive realization: ICESCR model — India moving toward statutory rights (Rajasthan RTH 2023). HEO understands constitutional architecture enables AND limits health rights。

question: 'One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC)' scheme के implementation में संघवाद की challenges और health-nutrition nexus को critically examine करें।

options.text: ONORC — state-designed scheme है, Centre की नहीं

ONORC (portability of PDS across states): migrant workers को nutrition security; states reluctant — revenue loss argument; SC intervention required; NFSA implementation variation; nutrition → health outcomes → HEO's cross-department coordination role
ONORC — केवल urban areas में applicable है
PDS — private sector द्वारा manage होता है

explanation: ONORC and Federalism-Health Nexus: One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC) — portability of NFSA entitlements across states using Aadhaar-seeded PDS. Significance: 80 crore beneficiaries can access PDS anywhere. Federalism challenges: (1) States reluctant — concern about financing migrants from other states, (2) Tamil Nadu, Chhattisgarh delayed; SC (Re: Migrant Workers case, 2021) directed compliance, (3) Implementation: ePoS machines, Aadhaar-PDS seeding — state capacity variation. Health-Nutrition nexus: (1) PDS access → food security → malnutrition prevention → IMR/MMR reduction, (2) Migrant workers' nutritional vulnerability → TB, anemia, diarrheal diseases, (3) NFSA: fortified rice, iodized salt — nutrition interventions through PDS. HEO's role: (1) NFSA-ICDS convergence, (2) Anganwadi-PDS integration for supplementary nutrition, (3) Identify nutrition-vulnerable migrant families. ONORC example shows health programming requires multi-state governance coordination。

question: भारत में 'Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA)' की health legislation में absence और इसके consequences को critically evaluate करें — PCPNDT, COTPA, Drugs Act amendments के reference में।

options.text: India में Regulatory Impact Assessment — mandatory है सभी health legislation में

RIA in India — absent or inadequate: PCPNDT amendments without sex-selective abortion trend impact analysis; COTPA without health economic model; Drugs price control without innovation disincentive study — evidence-free policy-making
Health legislation — technical departments द्वारा ही adequately evaluated होती है
RIA — World Bank द्वारा India को mandate किया गया है

explanation: Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) in Indian Health Legislation: RIA (international best practice): Before legislation/regulation, assess (1) Problem definition, (2) Objectives, (3) Options (regulatory + non-regulatory), (4) Costs and benefits, (5) Implementation challenges, (6) Monitoring. India's situation: (1) No mandatory RIA for health legislation, (2) Pre-legislative consultation (2014 Guidelines) — suggested but not enforced, (3) Standing Committee review post-introduction — often truncated. Case studies: (1) PCPNDT Amendment 2003: added mobile ultrasound regulation without impact assessment → legitimate diagnostic delays in rural areas, (2) COTPA 2003: no economic modeling → implementation cost underestimated → state enforcement weak, (3) Drugs (Prices) Control Order 2013: price ceilings without RIA on pharmaceutical innovation disincentive, (4) NMC Act 2020: stakeholder consultation inadequate (doctor protests). Need: Independent Regulatory Authority for Health (like TRAI for telecom) with mandatory RIA. HEO: advocates evidence-based policy, conducts local impact assessment。

question: भारत में 'Federalization of Health Emergencies' की challenges को critically examine करें — COVID में Centre-State coordination failures, IHR obligations, और NDMA-State SDMA conflicts।

options.text: COVID में Centre-State coordination — completely smooth था

COVID exposed federalism stress: NDMA central guidelines vs. state lockdown variations; oxygen allocation Centre-controlled but hospital operation state's; IHR reporting — Centre obligated (WHO) but state data quality varies; 'pandemic federalism' requires clearer constitutional framework
NDMA Act 2005 — states को pandemic response से exclude करता है
IHR obligations — state governments directly WHO को report करते हैं

explanation: COVID-19 Federalism Stress: Constitutional framework gaps: (1) No explicit 'health emergency' in constitution — NDMA Act 2005 (disaster) + Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 + DM Act state-level. NDMA-SDMA tensions: (1) National guidelines (lockdown, unlock phases) by NDMA (Centre) — states followed but varied implementation, (2) Oxygen crisis: Centre controlled oxygen allocation, industrial oxygen converted — but hospital administration = state, (3) Vaccine procurement: Centre negotiated but distribution = state; pricing disputes (Centre free + states paid model abandoned June 2021 after SC intervention). IHR Obligations: (1) WHO International Health Regulations (2005) — India as State Party; Centre (MoHFW) is IHR Focal Point; state data aggregated centrally, (2) IHR reporting to WHO — Centre's obligation; state data quality critical but uneven, (3) COVID data: state reporting inconsistencies (excess mortality debate). Reform suggestions: (1) Concurrent List 'Epidemic Control' entry, (2) Mandatory health data sharing protocol, (3) Pre-negotiated Centre-State resource sharing framework。

question: भारत में 'Social Audit' mechanism की constitutional और statutory basis को critically examine करें और MGNREGS social audit model को health sector में replicate करने की feasibility analyze करें।

options.text: Social Audit — केवल MGNREGS में statutory है और health में possible नहीं

Social Audit: MGNREGS Act 2005 Section 17 — statutory basis; health में NHRC guidelines + NHM community processes (VHSNC, Jan Sunwai) — non-statutory; health sector replication challenges: clinical quality vs. financial audit, medical knowledge gap in community
Social Audit — केवल financial irregularities detect करता है
MKSS model — government द्वारा developed किया गया था

explanation: Social Audit — Constitutional and Statutory Analysis: Constitutional basis: Art. 19(1)(a) — right to information; Art. 19(1)(b) — assembly; Art. 243G — Gram Panchayat development plans subject to community oversight. Statutory basis: MGNREGA Section 17 — mandatory social audit by gram sabha (SSAAT — Social Audit Unit at state level). MKSS model: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (Rajasthan) → Jan Sunwai (public hearing) → RTI movement → MGNREGS social audit. Health Sector: (1) NHM community processes: VHSNC (village health + sanitation + nutrition committee), Jan Arogya Samiti — non-statutory, (2) ASHA grievance committees, (3) NHRC recommendations on social audit of health facilities — not implemented. Feasibility challenges in health: (1) Clinical quality audit requires medical knowledge (wage register is simple; surgery outcome is not), (2) Data: HMIS not as transparent as MGNREGS MIS, (3) Power asymmetry: medical community resistance. Successful models: Rajasthan's Jatan Sansthan health Jan Sunwais, Chhattisgarh health social audit pilots。

question: 'PESA 1996 (Provisions of Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas)' और tribal health rights की governance को critically examine करें — Section 4 provisions और actual implementation gap।

options.text: PESA — Scheduled Areas में regular Panchayati Raj Act लागू करता है

PESA Section 4: Gram Sabha = competent → traditional medicine, NTFP including medicinal plants; states must pass conforming legislation; implementation gap — most states' PESA rules incomplete; tribal health governance = contested space
PESA — health से संबंधित कोई provision नहीं है
PESA ने 5th Schedule areas में all Central health schemes ban किए

explanation: PESA 1996 and Tribal Health Governance: PESA Section 4 key provisions for health: (1) Section 4(d): Gram Sabha shall be competent to safeguard and preserve traditions and customs, (2) Section 4(m)(ii): Gram Panchayat shall be consulted before acquisition of land for development projects (affects health facility land), (3) Section 4(m)(i): control over minor forest produce including medicinal plants — tribal traditional medicine systems, (4) Gram Sabha power: manage natural resources, minor water bodies. Implementation gaps: (1) Only 10 of 10 5th Schedule states passed conforming legislation — but most incomplete/weak, (2) Tribal health traditionalists vs. biomedical system conflict unresolved, (3) Health workers appointed by state (not gram sabha as intended), (4) NTFP commercialization harming medicinal plant access. Positive deviance: Tribal health plans by Gram Sabhas in some Maharashtra districts. HEO in tribal areas: must work within PESA framework — gram sabha approval for health camps, ASHA selection (traditionally should involve gram sabha)。

question: भारत में 'E-Governance in Health' की accountability paradox को critically examine करें — HMIS, NHA (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission), और surveillance-privacy-access trilemma।

options.text: Health e-governance — सभी problems solve करता है

HMIS: data quality vs. data entry burden paradox; ABDM: Health ID + ABHA — interoperability gain vs. surveillance risk (data leak, insurance discrimination); digital divide (rural, elderly, women) — exclusion risk; accountability ≠ automatically follow digitization
ABDM — government employee data only, public excluded
Digital health records — India में fully legal protection मिली है

explanation: E-Governance in Health — accountability paradox: HMIS (Health Management Information System): (1) Data quality-burden paradox: ANMs/ASHAs spend 40%+ time on data entry → burnout, (2) HMIS reports often inflated (100%+ immunization in some blocks), (3) Accountability: data exists but action on outliers weak. Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM): ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) — 14-digit health ID for longitudinal health records. Trilemma: (1) Interoperability gain: doctor can access records anywhere, (2) Surveillance risk: government can profile health behavior; insurance companies may discriminate on pre-existing conditions, (3) Exclusion risk: elderly, rural, women without smartphones/Aadhaar excluded from benefits. Legal framework: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 — some protection but health data = sensitive personal data; specific health data regulation pending. IT Act 2000 — inadequate for health data. HEO: champion digital inclusion, protect health data rights, ensure data accuracy not just volume。

question: भारत में 'National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)' की health rights enforcement mechanism की limitations को critically examine करें — recommendatory vs. binding orders और state government compliance।

options.text: NHRC — binding orders issue करता है और state compliance mandatory है

NHRC recommendations non-binding; health complaints: malnutrition deaths (Baran-Rajasthan), sterilization deaths — NHRC issues recommendations, states often ignore; 'toothless watchdog' critique vs. 'norm-setting' value; SHRC capacity variation
NHRC — health rights को specifically address नहीं करता
NHRC का jurisdiction — केवल armed forces complaints तक

explanation: NHRC and Health Rights Enforcement: NHRC (National Human Rights Commission) under Protection of Human Rights Act 1993: Composition: Retired CJI as Chairman. Health jurisdiction: (1) Takes up malnutrition cases (Baran, Rajasthan — starvation deaths 2001-02), (2) Sterilization camp deaths (Chhattisgarh 2014 — 15 deaths), (3) Health facility denial of care cases, (4) Drug quality concerns. Limitations: (1) Recommendations only — not binding orders; government must respond within 6-8 weeks, (2) Compliance mechanism: weak — states acknowledge but often don't implement, (3) Jurisdiction: cannot investigate Armed Forces, (4) Own motion: NHRC can act suo motu but lacks enforcement machinery. SHRC (State Human Rights Commissions): Capacity varies — some states' SHRCs not functional. 'Toothless watchdog' vs. 'norm-setting': (1) Sets standards, creates public pressure, (2) Some compliance — reimbursement to victims in sterilization cases. Compare: NHRC India vs. South Africa Human Rights Commission (binding recommendations) — India model is weaker。

question: भारत में 'Essential Services Maintenance Act (ESMA)' और health workers' right to strike के बीच constitutional tension को critically analyze करें।

options.text: Health workers को strike का अधिकार है जो कभी restrict नहीं हो सकता

ESMA under Concurrent List — states can declare health services 'essential'; Right to Strike = not explicit fundamental right (Art. 19(1)(c) = association only); SC held some strike rights via ILO conventions; ASHA wage strikes vs. state ESMA invocation — constitutional grey zone
ILO conventions — India में domestic law से higher status हैं
Health workers' strike — Art. 21 (Right to Health of patients) को override नहीं कर सकती

explanation: ESMA and Health Workers' Rights: Essential Services Maintenance Act (Central + State ESMAs): declares certain services essential → strike = illegal for 6 months. Health services: most states have notified hospitals, medical services as essential. Constitutional analysis: (1) Right to Strike: NOT explicit fundamental right; Art. 19(1)(c) = right to form associations; SC held right to strike is a statutory/legal right, not fundamental (Bank Nalini Case, Gujarat Steel Tubes), (2) ESMA invocation during doctor strikes (Rajasthan 2017, Delhi 2019 — ESMA threat), (3) ILO Conventions 87 and 98 (Freedom of Association) — India ratified ILO 87 partially; not ratified ILO 98. ASHA strikes (2019, 2022): ASHAs are 'volunteers' → ESMA technically inapplicable but state pressure used. Patient's Right (Art. 21) vs. Worker's Right (Art. 19/21): (1) No absolute patient right to specific doctor, (2) But essential emergency care must continue — partial work-to-rule vs. full strike distinction. HEO: facilitates grievance redressal to prevent health worker discontent→ strikes。

question: 'Compulsory Licensing (Section 84-92 of Patents Act 1970)' और 'Doha Declaration on TRIPS' को India की public health obligations के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें — Natco-Bayer से Bedaquiline तक।

options.text: India ने कभी compulsory license issue नहीं किया

India's first CL: Bayer-Natco (Sorafenib, 2012) — kidney cancer drug; Doha Declaration (2001): TRIPS flexibility — CL for public health; India Section 3(d) — evergreening prevention; Bedaquiline (TB drug) — government use order route; IP vs. Access tension ongoing
Doha Declaration — TRIPS को completely override करती है
Compulsory Licensing — केवल generic drug companies के लिए है

explanation: Compulsory Licensing and Public Health: Patents Act 1970 (amended 2005 — TRIPS compliance): Section 84: CL grounds — (1) not reasonably available, (2) not available at affordable price, (3) not worked in India. Section 92: Government use license — no CL application needed, government can use any patent for public purpose. India's CL history: (1) Natco Pharma v. Bayer (2012) — first CL for Sorafenib (kidney cancer); price ₹2.8 lakh vs. ₹8750 (Natco). Doha Declaration (2001): TRIPS must be interpreted to protect public health; CL allowed for public health emergencies; compulsory import for countries with no manufacturing capacity. India-specific: Section 3(d) — prevents evergreening (modified forms of known substances must show enhanced efficacy — Novartis Gleevec denied patent, 2013). Bedaquiline (TB drug — MDR-TB): government use order (Section 92) being explored; voluntary license by Johnson & Johnson for low-income countries. Ongoing tension: USA pressure (Special 301 report) vs. India's public health commitments。

question: भारत में 'National Action Plan for Climate Change (NAPCC) 2008' और health outcomes के बीच की linkage को critically examine करें — NCAP, NAPA, और health sector adaptation।

options.text: NAPCC 2008 में health mission नहीं है

NAPCC 8 missions: National Mission for Sustainable Habitat — indirect health; NO dedicated health mission; NDMA-Health convergence for climate disasters; NCAP (National Clean Air Programme 2019) — AQI, health outcomes; health sector adaptation plans emerging but not mainstreamed
NAPCC directly health outcomes को guarantee करता है
Climate change — India में health emergency declare करने का basis है

explanation: NAPCC and Health — Critical Analysis: NAPCC 2008 (National Action Plan on Climate Change): 8 National Missions — Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge. No explicit health mission — gap. Health impacts of climate change in India: (1) Heat stress → heat stroke (2022 — 400+ deaths), (2) Vector-borne: dengue, malaria range expansion (altitude, geography), (3) Air pollution (PM2.5, ozone) → respiratory, cardiovascular, (4) Food insecurity (crop failure) → malnutrition. NCAP (2019): PM10/PM2.5 reduction targets in 132 cities; no direct health outcome targets but implied. NAPA (National Adaptation Plan — state level): health sector adaptation plans → disease surveillance, heat action plans (Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan 2013 — mortality reduction evidence). Health sector gaps: (1) Climate health vulnerability mapping, (2) Climate-resilient health infrastructure, (3) Health worker training on climate diseases. IPCC + India Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change 2021 — evidence base。

question: भारत में 'Right to Health' को Fundamental Right के रूप में कैसे evolved किया गया है — Art. 21, Paschim Banga Case, और Consumer Education Case के संदर्भ में critically examine करें।

options.text: Right to Health — Constitution में explicitly listed Fundamental Right है

Right to Health = Art. 21 (Right to Life) का implied part; Paschim Banga (1996) — state obligated to provide emergency healthcare; Consumer Education (1995) — right to health = fundamental; DPSP Art. 47 + Art. 21 together create justiciable health obligation
Art. 47 (DPSP) alone provides enforceable right to health
Right to Health — केवल PIL के through enforce होता है, High Courts jurisdiction नहीं

explanation: Evolution of Right to Health as Fundamental Right: Art. 21: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' SC expanded 'life' to include dignified living. Key cases: (1) Vincent Panikurlangara v. Union of India (1987): right to health and medical care = fundamental right integral to Art. 21; (2) Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of WB (1996): denial of emergency medical treatment = violation of Art. 21; state must provide emergency care; (3) Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India (1995): right to health of workers = fundamental right. Art. 47 (DPSP): state duty to raise level of nutrition and standard of living; improvement of public health. Art. 47 read with Art. 21 = stronger judicial basis. International: ICESCR Art. 12 (right to highest attainable standard of health) — India ratified; used by courts for interpretation (Vishaka principle). Limitations: positive obligation — courts reluctant to order resource allocation (separation of powers); emergency care clearly enforceable, routine care less clear.

question: 'Concurrent List Entry 6' (Public Health) और Entry 26 (Medical Professions) के बीच Centre-State jurisdiction conflict को critically analyze करें — NMC Act 2020 और Clinical Establishments Act 2010 के आलोक में।

options.text: स्वास्थ्य — केवल State List का विषय है

State List Entry 11 (Public Health) + Concurrent List Entry 26 (Medical Profession); NMC Act 2020 — central regulation via Entry 66 (Coordination in higher education); CEA 2010 — Concurrent, state adoption voluntary; fragmented regulation across centre-state
All health matters — Union List में हैं
Clinical Establishments Act — सभी states में mandatory है

explanation: Constitutional Distribution of Health Powers: State List Entry 11: Public Health and Sanitation; Hospitals and Dispensaries. Concurrent List Entry 26: Legal, Medical and other Professions (regulation). Concurrent List Entry 25: Education including medical education — Centre + State (Entry 66: Coordination and standards in higher education = Central power). NMC Act 2020: Uses Entry 66 to establish National Medical Commission — central body replacing MCI; regulates medical education standards. Clinical Establishments Act (CEA) 2010: Uses Concurrent List; NOT mandatory — states must adopt separately; as of 2024: many major states (Maharashtra, TN, Kerala, Karnataka) NOT adopted; only ~11 states adopted. Fragmentation: (1) Medical education = central (NMC); (2) Practice regulation = state medical councils + central NMC coordination; (3) Hospital regulation = CEA (if adopted) or state-specific acts; (4) Public health = state; (5) Drug regulation = central (CDSCO). HEO must navigate this layered jurisdiction in field work.

question: भारत में 'Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health' की oversight role को critically evaluate करें — committee reports का policy impact और executive accountability।

options.text: Parliamentary Committees — executive को binding instructions दे सकती हैं

Standing Committee on Health: scrutinizes Ministry budget + bills + performance; reports recommendatory; notable reports — NMC Bill, drug pricing, AMR; government submits ATRs; public record pressure = real accountability; but no enforcement power
Standing Committee — केवल budget allocation decide करती है
Committee reports — automatically law बन जाती हैं

explanation: Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare: Composition: ~30 MPs (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha). Functions: (1) Examine demands for grants, (2) Scrutinize bills referred by Speaker/Chairman, (3) Examine policies and performance of Ministry of Health and AYUSH. Notable reports: (1) NMC Bill 2019 — committee recommended major changes (bridge course controversy); some incorporated; (2) Anti-microbial resistance — comprehensive report 2021; (3) Drug pricing and NPPA functioning; (4) Mental healthcare implementation; (5) COVID-19 response. Accountability mechanism: Government must submit Action Taken Reports (ATR) — but no penalty for non-compliance. Real accountability: (1) Public record — media attention; (2) Reputational cost on minister; (3) Institutionalizes opposition scrutiny. Limitations: (1) Committee cannot enforce; (2) Government often rejects recommendations claiming policy prerogative; (3) Limited technical expertise of MPs. HEO relevance: Committee reports shape program priorities (NHM, TB, mental health) that guide field implementation.

question: 'RTI Act 2005' का स्वास्थ्य क्षेत्र में accountability mechanism के रूप में critically evaluate करें — third party, commercial confidence, और fiduciary exemptions।

options.text: RTI Act — health sector में पूरी तरह लागू होता है, कोई exemption नहीं

RTI health applications: drug approvals (CDSCO), NRHM fund utilization (UP NRHM scam 2011 exposed); Section 8 exemptions — commercial confidence (pharma trade secrets), fiduciary (patient privacy); SC: patient health records = third party info; larger public interest override possible
Private hospitals — RTI के अंतर्गत नहीं आते कभी भी
CDSCO drug approval records — completely exempt from RTI

explanation: RTI Act 2005 and Health Sector: Section 2(h): Public Authority = any authority established by Constitution, law, or substantially funded by government. Health applications: (1) CDSCO drug approvals — clinical trial data, approval basis; (2) NRHM fund utilization — UP NRHM scam (2011); (3) District Hospital performance, staffing; (4) NHM ASHA incentives. Section 8 exemptions: (1) 8(1)(d): commercial confidence, trade secrets — pharma companies use to block trial data disclosure; (2) 8(1)(j): personal information, unwarranted invasion of privacy — patient records, HIV status; (3) 8(1)(e): information available in fiduciary capacity — doctor-patient relationship = fiduciary; patient health records = exempt. SC in Girish Ramchandra Deshpande (2012): personal medical records = personal information; disclosure requires public interest justification. Larger public interest override (Proviso to 8(1)): CDSCO approval data of controversial drugs — public interest can override. Private hospitals: NOT public authority unless substantially funded/controlled. HEO: can use RTI to access health program data, expose gaps.

question: भारत में 'Public Interest Litigation (PIL)' का health rights enforcement में historical role critically examine करें — judicial activism के benefits और pitfalls।

options.text: PIL — health rights में inapplicable है

PIL transformed health rights: Paschim Banga (emergency care), Vincent (drug quality), Murli Deora (smoking in public places 2001); judicial activism gains — access to justice; pitfalls — judicial overreach, policy-making by courts, implementation deficit; SC tried to curb frivolous PIL
PIL — केवल High Courts में file हो सकती है
PIL के outcomes — हमेशा implement होते हैं

explanation: PIL and Health Rights in India: Origins: P.N. Bhagwati J. and V.R. Krishna Iyer J. — 'epistolary jurisdiction' (letter treated as PIL); relaxed locus standi. Key health PILs: (1) Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) — emergency care obligation; (2) Vincent Panikurlangara — drug quality standards; (3) Murli Deora v. Union of India (2001) — SC banned smoking in public places before COTPA 2003; (4) Almitra Patel — municipal solid waste management (SWM Rules 2000); (5) MC Mehta series — air/water pollution. Benefits: (1) Access to justice for poor, voiceless; (2) Policy reform where legislature inactive; (3) Real-time accountability. Pitfalls: (1) Judicial overreach — courts dictating administrative details; (2) Policy domain invasion (separation of powers); (3) Implementation deficit — orders not monitored; (4) PIL industry — frivolous filings; (5) Court cannot manage hospitals/health systems. SC imposed costs on frivolous PILs. HEO: understands PIL as accountability mechanism but also its limitations.

question: 'Mental Healthcare Act 2017' की rights-based approach को critically evaluate करें — Section 18, advance directives, और implementation gap।

options.text: MHA 2017 — केवल forced treatment को regulate करता है

MHA 2017: rights-based (UNCRPD-aligned); Section 18 — right to treatment without discrimination; advance directive (Section 5-11); Section 115 — suicide attempt decriminalized; BUT: SMHA formation incomplete, psychiatrist shortage (0.3/100,000), community mental health underfunded
MHA 2017 — Concurrent List के under है इसलिए states exempt हैं
Advance Directives under MHA 2017 — courts cannot override

explanation: Mental Healthcare Act 2017 — Critical Analysis: Framework: UNCRPD (UN Convention on Rights of Persons with Disabilities) — India ratified 2007; MHA 2017 aligns with it, replacing MHA 1987. Key rights provisions: (1) Section 18: Right to treatment without discrimination; (2) Section 19: Right to equality; (3) Section 20: Right to live in community; (4) Section 115: Attempt to suicide — person presumed to have mental illness; shall not be punished under IPC Section 309. Advance Directives (Sections 5-11): Person can specify treatment preferences while competent → valid during incapacity. SMHA (State Mental Health Authority): Many states non-compliant. Mental Health Review Board: Oversight of admission/treatment decisions; functioning poor. Implementation gaps: (1) SMHA not constituted in many states; (2) Acute shortage of psychiatrists (0.3/100,000 vs WHO recommended 3); (3) Advance directive awareness near-zero; (4) Community mental health underfunded. IPC Section 309 anomaly: MHA 2017 says no punishment but IPC not yet amended.

question: भारत में 'PC-PNDT Act 1994' की implementation failures को critically analyze करें — SRB data, Appropriate Authority, और enforcement paradoxes।

options.text: PC-PNDT Act — completely successful रहा है

PC-PNDT 1994 (amended 2003): bans sex selection; SRB = 929/1000 males (NFHS-5) — marginal improvement; Appropriate Authority weak — understaffed, conflict of interest; technology race (portable USG, telemedicine sex determination); Haryana SRB 836 still worst; demand-side son preference deep cultural norm
PC-PNDT Act — केवल abortion को regulate करता है
SRB improvement — PC-PNDT की failure का evidence नहीं है

explanation: PC-PNDT Act 1994 — Implementation Analysis: Act provisions: (1) Ban on sex determination of fetus; (2) Mandatory registration of ultrasound facilities; (3) Appropriate Authority (AA) — district level — registration + inspection; (4) Punishment: 3-5 years imprisonment, ₹10,000-50,000 fine; (5) 2003 Amendment: included pre-conception sex selection techniques. SRB data: NFHS-3 (2005-06): 914 boys/1000 girls; NFHS-5 (2019-21): 929 — marginal improvement; states vary: Haryana 836 (worst), Kerala 955 (best). Implementation failures: (1) AA understaffed, conflict of interest; (2) Inspections nominal; (3) Conviction rate extremely low; (4) Technology race: portable USG, telemedicine; (5) 'Decoy operations' — some states successful (Maharashtra, Rajasthan). Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015): behavior change campaign targeting 100 districts with worst SRB — mixed evidence. Demand side: son preference = deep cultural norm — law alone insufficient. HEO: community sensitization on daughter valuation; mandatory reporting culture.

question: 'MTP Act 1971 and 2021 Amendment' को women's reproductive autonomy और Puttaswamy privacy rights के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: MTP Act — women को unconditional abortion का right देता है

MTP 1971: doctor-centric (one/two RMP opinion); 2021 Amendment: 20→24 weeks for special categories (rape, disability, minors); Medical Board for >24 weeks; SC 2022 (X v. Principal Secretary) — unmarried women included; Puttaswamy = reproductive autonomy as privacy; IPC 312 still exists — provider risk
MTP 2021 Amendment — abortion को completely decriminalize करती है
MTP Act — केवल married women पर apply होता है

explanation: MTP Act 1971 and 2021 Amendment — Critical Analysis: MTP 1971: Termination allowed up to 12 weeks (one RMP opinion) and 12-20 weeks (two RMP opinions); grounds — contraceptive failure (married women), rape, fetal abnormality, risk to woman's life/health. 2021 Amendment: (1) Upper limit: 20→24 weeks for special categories — survivors of rape/sexual assault, minors, differently-abled women, fetal anomalies detected late, change in marital status; (2) >24 weeks: Medical Board of experts decides. SC in X v. Principal Secretary, Health & FW, Govt. of NCT of Delhi (2022): 2021 amendment applies to all women including unmarried; reproductive choice under Art. 21 (privacy — Puttaswamy). Key critique: Doctor-centric, not woman-centric — RMP has final say, not woman's autonomous choice. IPC Section 312 (miscarriage) still exists — providers face criminal risk. Puttaswamy (2017): bodily integrity + reproductive choices = privacy core. Compare: USA post-Roe reversal (2022) — India's framework is more protective.

question: 'Puttaswamy Judgment 2017' (Right to Privacy) का health data governance पर impact — ABDM, DPDP Act 2023 के संदर्भ में critically analyze करें।

options.text: Puttaswamy judgment — health data को directly regulate करता है

Puttaswamy 2017 (9-judge bench): Privacy = fundamental right under Art. 21; health data = sensitive personal data; ABDM/ABHA consent framework required; DPDP Act 2023 — health data = 'sensitive'; government exemptions (national security, public health) — broad concern; no specific health data law yet
Puttaswamy judgment — केवल financial data पर apply होता है
DPDP Act 2023 — health data को specially protect नहीं करता

explanation: Puttaswamy and Health Data: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — 9-judge constitutional bench: Privacy = fundamental right under Art. 21; not absolute — subject to reasonable restrictions. Health data dimensions: (1) Bodily integrity: right to refuse medical treatment; (2) Informational privacy: health records, HIV status, mental health history; (3) Reproductive autonomy: family planning choices. ABDM (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission) and ABHA: Health ID; digital health records; consent framework — patient must consent to share records. DPDP Act 2023: health data = 'sensitive personal data'; requires explicit consent for processing; Data Protection Board for redressal; government exemptions broad — concern. No specific Health Data Protection legislation in India (unlike EU GDPR with health-specific rules). Risks: (1) Insurance discrimination using ABHA data; (2) Government health profiling; (3) Genetic data protection inadequate. HEO: informed consent for health data use; right to know, right to correct health records.

question: 'Consumer Protection Act 2019' में medical services की liability — IMA v. VP Shantha (1995) और Jacob Mathew (2005) के संदर्भ में critically trace करें।

options.text: Medical services — Consumer Protection Act के अंतर्गत कभी नहीं आए

IMA v. VP Shantha (1995): SC — medical services = 'service' under COPRA; 'deficiency in service' standard; free service = excluded; Jacob Mathew (2005) — high threshold for IPC 304A (criminal negligence); 2019 Act: enhanced jurisdiction, e-filing; government hospital coverage = unclear
2019 Act ने medical services को COPRA से बाहर कर दिया
Government hospitals — COPRA के अंतर्गत कभी liable नहीं हैं

explanation: Consumer Protection and Medical Services: IMA v. VP Shantha (1995): SC 3-judge bench — Medical practitioners offering services for consideration = 'service' under Consumer Protection Act 1986; 'deficiency in service' (not mere negligence — higher threshold); free services (charitable/government without fee) = excluded. Consumer Protection Act 2019: (1) District (up to ₹1 crore), State (₹1-10 crore), National (above ₹10 crore); (2) E-filing complaints; (3) Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA); (4) Product liability (medical devices). Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005): High threshold for criminal medical negligence (IPC 304A) — gross negligence only; protects good faith medical decisions. Challenges: (1) Long pendency at commissions; (2) IMA contests jurisdiction; (3) Government hospital coverage — unclear if paid services covered. SC examining whether medical services should have special regime. HEO relevance: patient rights to redressal; IEC on consumer rights in healthcare.

question: भारत में 'SC/ST/OBC health access inequality' को constitutional remedies और caste discrimination के संदर्भ में critically examine करें।

options.text: Reservation in medical colleges — health access inequality को directly solve करता है

NFHS-5: SC IMR 43.8, ST IMR 44.4 vs national 35.2; reservations in medical education (15% SC, 7.5% ST, 27% OBC) = supply-side; Lancet 2018 documented caste discrimination in public hospitals; Art. 17 + PCR Act 1955 + SC/ST PoA Act 1989; SCSP/TSP budget allocations; structural discrimination = key barrier
India में caste-based health discrimination — documented नहीं है
SC/ST Sub-Plan — health programs में applicable नहीं है

explanation: Caste and Health — Constitutional Analysis: Data (NFHS-5): SC IMR: 43.8 vs general 35.2; ST IMR: 44.4; ST child stunting 42.3% vs National 35.5%. Constitutional provisions: Art. 15(4): special provisions for SC/ST/OBC; Art. 17: Abolition of untouchability; Art. 46: State to promote SC/ST interests. Reservation: 15% SC, 7.5% ST at central institutions; 27% OBC (post-Indra Sawhney). SCSP/TSP (Scheduled Caste Sub-Plan/Tribal Sub-Plan): budget allocation proportional to SC/ST population for their development including health. Documented discrimination: Lancet study (2018) — caste discrimination in public hospitals (SC/OBC patients wait longer, lower quality care); Dalit women face discrimination in MCH services. PCR Act 1955, SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act 1989: discrimination in access to public places including hospitals = penal offence. HEO: alert to caste-based denial of health services; facilitates access for marginalized communities.

question: 'RPWD Act 2016' के health provisions को Section 25, 'reasonable accommodation', और UNCRPD alignment के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: RPWD Act 2016 — केवल employment और education को cover करता है

RPWD 2016 Section 25: free healthcare in government institutions; 21 specified disabilities (expanded from 7); reasonable accommodation obligation on health facilities; UNCRPD Art. 25 aligned; BUT: accessible hospitals rare, disability health schemes budget inadequate, mental illness + disability dual jurisdiction challenge
RPWD Act 2016 — private hospitals पर apply नहीं होता
UNCRPD — India के domestic law में directly enforceable है

explanation: RPWD Act 2016 and Health Rights: Replaced Persons with Disabilities Act 1995; aligns with UNCRPD (ratified by India 2007). Key expansion: 7 → 21 specified disabilities (including mental illness, autism, cerebral palsy, thalassemia, acid attack victims). Section 25 health provisions: (1) Free healthcare in government hospitals; (2) Healthcare not to be denied on basis of disability; (3) States to formulate schemes; (4) Accessible health facilities and equipment. Reasonable Accommodation (Section 2(y)): necessary modifications without imposing disproportionate burden; priority queuing, sign language interpreters, accessible examination tables. UNCRPD Art. 25: Right to health without discrimination; right to sexual/reproductive health. Implementation gaps: (1) Most government hospitals non-accessible (ramps, accessible toilets); (2) Rehabilitation services inadequate; (3) ADIP scheme (Assistive Devices) — limited reach; (4) Mental illness listed as disability — MHA 2017 + RPWD simultaneously challenging. Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities: quasi-judicial complaints mechanism.

question: भारत में 'Tribal Health Governance' को Fifth Schedule, PESA 1996, और Forest Rights Act 2006 के आलोक में critically analyze करें।

options.text: 5th Schedule Areas में Central health schemes बिना modification directly लागू होती हैं

5th Schedule: Governor + Tribes Advisory Council; PESA: Gram Sabha competent for health governance, NTFP (medicinal plants); FRA 2006 — Community Forest Rights; tribal health worst (ST IMR 44.4, stunting 42.3%); THSP inadequate; Shyam Agarwal Committee (2018) documented major gaps
Forest Rights Act 2006 — tribal health से completely unrelated है
Governor 5th Schedule Areas में Centre को override करने वाले health orders issue कर सकते हैं

explanation: Tribal Health Governance — Constitutional Analysis: Fifth Schedule (Art. 244): Governor's special powers in Scheduled Areas; Tribes Advisory Council (TAC); Governor can direct/exclude Central and State laws. PESA 1996: Gram Sabha = key institution; traditional medicine systems, NTFP (medicinal plants) = Gram Sabha jurisdiction; ASHA selection. Forest Rights Act 2006: Community Forest Rights — NTFP collection including medicinal plants → traditional healers empowered. Tribal health status: NFHS-5 ST IMR 44.4 (national 35.2); stunting 42.3% (national 35.5%); malaria — tribal belts disproportionate burden. Gaps: (1) THSP budget inadequate; (2) PVTG (75 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups) — special health packages needed; (3) Mobile Medical Units — coverage poor; (4) Doctors reluctant to post in remote tribal areas. High-Level Committee on Tribal Health (Shyam Agarwal 2018): major gaps documented — recommended tribal health policy. HEO in tribal areas: gram sabha-based health planning, traditional medicine integration.

question: भारत में 'CAG health sector audit' की policy impact को critically evaluate करें — performance audit, NHM accountability, और UP NRHM scam।

options.text: CAG — health sector में audit नहीं करती

CAG (Art. 148-151): compliance + performance audit; NHM audit reports — unspent balances, ASHA incentive delays; UP NRHM scam (2011) — CAG findings triggered CBI; PM-JAY fraud audit; PAC parliamentary follow-up; retrospective accountability; direct enforcement = nil
CAG reports — government को directly bind करती हैं
CAG — केवल central government programs audit करती है, state health programs नहीं

explanation: CAG and Health Sector Accountability: Constitutional basis: Art. 148-151 — CAG = independent constitutional body; audits accounts of Union and States. Types: (1) Compliance/regularity audit; (2) Performance audit — programs achieved stated objectives; (3) Financial audit — accounts accurate. Key CAG health reports: (1) NHM performance audit — unspent balances, ASHA incentive delays (up to 6 months), drug procurement irregularities; (2) UP NRHM scam: CAG findings triggered CBI investigation — ₹5,000+ crore misappropriation; multiple officials arrested; (3) PM-JAY — fraud detection gaps; (4) AIIMS — procurement irregularities. Public Accounts Committee (PAC): Parliamentary committee examines CAG reports; calls secretaries; ATRs required. Real policy impact: (1) NHM fund flow reform; (2) Drug procurement centralization; (3) Accountability for health officials. Limitations: (1) Retrospective — reports come 2-3 years after expenditure; (2) Not real-time; (3) PAC — political dynamics.

question: भारत में 'Lokpal Act 2013' और Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 का health sector corruption में critically examine करें।

options.text: Lokpal — health sector corruption में investigate नहीं कर सकता

Lokpal 2013: PM+Ministers+MPs+Group A officers jurisdiction; PCA 1988 (amended 2018): both bribe giver AND taker liable; health corruption — drug procurement kickbacks, ghost ASHAs, PM-JAY fraud (₹491 crore detected); Section 17A — prior sanction shield; under-prosecution; Whistleblower Protection Act 2014 — poor implementation
PCA 1988 — केवल demand side (bribe taker) को punish करता है
Lokpal — state government health officials को cover नहीं करता

explanation: Anti-Corruption Framework in Health: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013: Lokpal — PM (with exceptions), Union Ministers, MPs, Group A/B/C/D central officers; Lokayuktas — state equivalent. Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 (amended 2018): (1) Bribe GIVER also liable (Section 8) unless coerced; (2) Section 17A — preliminary inquiry + prior sanction before FIR for officials — shield. Health corruption typology: (1) Drug procurement kickbacks (rigged tenders); (2) Ghost workers — fake ASHAs/ANMs on payroll; (3) PM-JAY fraud — ₹491 crore fake hospitalization claims detected by NHA 2019-2022; (4) Drug diversion — government medicines sold in private market; (5) UP NRHM scam — ₹5,000+ crore. Challenges: (1) Section 17A shield; (2) Long trials; (3) Whistleblower Protection Act 2014 — implementation poor; health whistleblowers vulnerable. Social audit as anti-corruption tool: MGNREGS model → health extension.

question: भारत में 'Tobacco Control Policy' को FCTC obligations, COTPA 2003, और Article 5.3 के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: India — WHO FCTC signatory नहीं है

India ratified FCTC 2004; COTPA 2003: cigarettes + smokeless tobacco regulated; FCTC Art. 5.3 — health policy must be protected from tobacco industry interference; India: 85% pictorial warnings (global leader); beedi — 7 crore worker economic-health tension; industry lobbying documented; EVPBA 2019 — e-cigarettes banned
COTPA 2003 — beedi को completely regulate करता है
FCTC obligations — India में enforceable नहीं हैं

explanation: Tobacco Control — FCTC and COTPA: WHO FCTC — India signed 2003, ratified 2004. FCTC obligations: (1) Tax increases (Art. 6); (2) Smoke-free public places (Art. 8); (3) Pictorial health warnings ≥50% of pack (Art. 11); (4) Ban on advertising, promotion, sponsorship (Art. 13); (5) Art. 5.3 — protect public health policy from tobacco industry vested interests. COTPA 2003: (1) Prohibition of smoking in public places; (2) Ban on sale to minors; (3) Pictorial warnings (India 85% — global leader); (4) Ban on surrogate advertising. Implementation challenges: (1) Beedi — cottage industry, 7 crore workers (predominantly SC/women) — economic-health policy tension; (2) Smokeless tobacco (gutkha, khaini) — state bans but leakage; (3) Art. 5.3 violation documented — tobacco industry in government committees; (4) EVPBA 2019 — e-cigarettes banned by executive order. HEO: tobacco cessation counselling (quitline 1800-11-2356), school-level prevention IEC.

question: भारत में 'Drug Regulation' को critically examine करें — CDSCO, D&C Act 1940, NDCT Rules 2019, और regulatory capture का जोखिम।

options.text: CDSCO — state drug controllers के साथ कोई coordination नहीं करता

D&C Act 1940: Central (CDSCO — new drug approval, manufacturing standards) + State (licensing, retail, distribution); NDCT Rules 2019 — EC registration, audio-visual consent, mandatory compensation for trial injury; regulatory capture risk — revolving door; Mashelkar Committee recommendations partially implemented; 59th Parliamentary report documented CDSCO-industry nexus
New Drug approval — exclusively State Drug Controller करता है
Clinical trials in India — completely unregulated हैं

explanation: Drug Regulation in India — Critical Analysis: Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940: Central (CDSCO): New drug approvals, import licenses, manufacturing standards, medical devices; State Drug Controllers: Manufacturing licenses, retail licenses, distribution, quality testing. NDCT Rules 2019: (1) Ethics Committees (EC) — registered with CDSCO; (2) Audio-visual informed consent; (3) Compensation for trial-related injury/death (mandatory formula); (4) New drug definition expanded (biologicals, biosimilars). Regulatory capture risk: (1) Revolving door — CDSCO officials → pharma industry; (2) Industry-funded studies submitted for approval; (3) Mashelkar Committee (2003) — recommended CDSCO autonomy; (4) 59th Standing Committee Report (2012) — CDSCO 'nexus' with pharma industry documented. Reforms needed: (1) Central Drug Authority (independent of Health Ministry); (2) Mandatory clinical trial data transparency; (3) Post-market surveillance strengthening. HEO: reports adverse drug reactions, monitors drug quality at facility level.

question: भारत में 'Surrogacy Act 2021 और ART Act 2021' को reproductive rights और health ethics के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: Commercial surrogacy — India में अभी भी legal है

Surrogacy Act 2021: commercial surrogacy banned; altruistic (close relative) surrogacy only; married Indian citizens eligible; ART Act 2021: ART clinics regulated; national registry; sex selection banned; LGBTQ+ और single women excluded — SC Supriyo 2023 (no FR to same-sex marriage) upheld exclusion; bodily autonomy of surrogate — inadequate compensation
ART Act 2021 — LGBTQ+ couples को surrogacy rights देता है
Surrogacy Board — decisions binding नहीं हैं

explanation: Surrogacy and ART Acts 2021 — Critical Analysis: Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021: (1) Commercial surrogacy banned; (2) Altruistic surrogacy only — 'close relative' surrogate; (3) Intending couple: married Indian citizens; (4) National Surrogacy Board (NSB) + State Surrogacy Boards. ART Regulation Act 2021: (1) ART clinics must register; (2) National ART and Surrogacy Registry; (3) Sex selection in ART = banned; (4) Gamete donors regulated. Rights critique: (1) SC in Supriyo v. Union of India (2023) — no fundamental right to marry for same-sex couples; ART/Surrogacy exclusion of LGBTQ+ upheld; (2) Single women — reproductive choice restricted; (3) Bodily autonomy of surrogate — compensation (medical expenses + insurance) inadequate. Positive: Exploitation of poor women as commercial surrogates reduced. Ethical tensions: commodification vs. autonomy; altruistic vs. commercial spectrum.

question: भारत में 'FSSAI Act 2006' और food safety की health protection role को critically examine करें — enforcement mechanism, adulteration prosecution, और 'Eat Right India'।

options.text: FSSAI — केवल packaged foods को regulate करती है

FSSAI Act 2006: consolidated 8 food laws; FBO license + registration; 3-tier enforcement (Central-State-Local FSO); FSO understaffed; adulteration prosecution rate low; penalty: life imprisonment + ₹10 lakh for death cases; Eat Right India — demand-side; traditional food controversy
FSSAI — drug safety भी regulate करती है
State governments — food safety में कोई role नहीं रखते

explanation: FSSAI and Health Protection: Food Safety and Standards Act 2006: Replaced 8 separate laws (Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954, etc.). Three-tier enforcement: (1) Central level (FSSAI): policy, standards, coordination; (2) State level: Designated Officer, Food Safety Commissioner; (3) Local: Food Safety Officers (FSO) — inspection, sampling, prosecution. Key provisions: (1) License for manufacturers (annual turnover ≥₹12 lakh), Registration for small sellers; (2) Food Recall mechanism; (3) Penalty: imprisonment up to life + ₹10 lakh fine for adulteration causing death. Challenges: (1) FSO:Population ratio inadequate; (2) NABL accredited food labs insufficient; (3) Prosecution rate low — mostly small traders; (4) Organic certification fraud. 'FSSAI vs. traditional food' controversy: FSSAI regulations on mithai, street food — contested. Eat Right India: FSSAI behavior change campaign. HEO: food adulteration health IEC; food safety-maternal/child nutrition link.

question: भारत में 'Cooperative Federalism' के health governance में application को critically examine करें — GST Council as model और health domain coordination failures।

options.text: GST Council model — health में already replicating हो रहा है

Cooperative Federalism in health: dedicated institution absent; ISC (Art. 263) — rarely used; GST Council (Centre+States equal voice) could inspire 'National Health Council' with deliberative power; COVID exposed coordination gap (oxygen, vaccines, lockdown); NHM conditional grants reduce state fiscal autonomy; Sarkaria + Punchhi Commission recommendations unimplemented
Inter-State Council — health matters specifically handle करता है regularly
Health — Concurrent List means Centre always dominant over states

explanation: Cooperative Federalism in Health — Critical Analysis: Constitutional basis: Health = primarily State List (Entry 11), Concurrent List (Entry 26 — Medical Professions) + Centre's fiscal dominance. Existing coordination mechanisms: (1) National Health Mission — conditional grants; states submit PIPs; Centre approves; reduces state autonomy; (2) Central Council of Health and Family Welfare: meets irregularly; recommendations non-binding; (3) ISC — rarely convened on health. COVID coordination failures: Exposed federalism stress — oxygen allocation (Centre-controlled, hospital operation = state), vaccine pricing disputes (Centre free + states paid model abandoned June 2021 after SC intervention). GST Council as model: Centre (1/3 votes) + States (2/3 votes); decisions by 3/4 majority; strong deliberative institution. No health equivalent. NHM fiscal federalism: 60:40 Centre:State (general), 90:10 (NE); matching share constrains smaller states. Reform need: Permanent National Health Council with real deliberative authority.

question: भारत में '73rd/74th Constitutional Amendment' और PRIs की health decentralization में role को critically evaluate करें — 3 Fs problem।

options.text: 73rd Amendment ने health को states से panchayats को mandatory transfer किया

73rd Amendment (1992): Schedule 11 Item 25 — health and sanitation = PRI function (discretionary, not mandatory); devolution = state decides; 3 Fs (funds, functions, functionaries) not fully transferred; Kerala = model devolution; VHSNC (NHM) = decentralization attempt; VHSNC non-statutory weakness
74th Amendment — municipal health functions को mandatory बनाता है
Gram Panchayat — CHC directly manage कर सकते हैं

explanation: 73rd/74th Amendment and Health Decentralization: 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992): (1) Three-tier Panchayati Raj — Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad; (2) Schedule 11: 29 functions — Item 25: Health and Sanitation, Family Welfare. Key word 'may' — devolution = discretionary, not mandatory. 74th Amendment: Urban Local Bodies (municipalities) — Schedule 12: 18 functions including urban health. 3 Fs problem: (1) Functions — most states transferred nominally but not substantively; (2) Funds — tied grants; panchayats rarely get untied health funds; (3) Functionaries — ANM/ASHA reporting lines = state, not panchayat. State variation: Kerala: People's Campaign for Decentralised Planning (1996) — health planning by gram sabha; model. NHM's decentralization: (1) VHSNC (village level): Untied Funds ₹10,000/village; (2) Rogi Kalyan Samiti (RKS): facility-level community governance. VHSNC weaknesses: (1) Not statutory; (2) Gram Sabha not always convened; (3) ASHA = secretary of VHSNC but tasks not fully operationalized.

question: भारत में '15th Finance Commission health grants' और fiscal federalism को critically analyze करें — conditionalities और state fiscal autonomy।

options.text: Finance Commission — health को directly fund नहीं करता

15th FC (2020-25): ₹70,051 crore health grants over 5 years; first time FC dedicated health grants; conditionalities — State Finance Commission, ULB health mandate; routed through PRIs and ULBs; BUT conditionalities reduce state autonomy; NHM grants separate stream; smaller states capacity constraints
Finance Commission health grants — NHM के साथ merge हो जाती हैं
15th FC health grants — केवल rural health infrastructure के लिए हैं

explanation: 15th Finance Commission and Health: 15th FC Report (2020-25): First time FC made dedicated health sector grants. Key elements: (1) ₹70,051 crore health grants over 5 years (2021-26); (2) Focused on strengthening primary healthcare; (3) Routed through PRIs and Urban Local Bodies; (4) Conditionalities: State Finance Commission established, urban local bodies must have own health mandate. Fiscal federalism implications: (1) Vertical imbalance: Centre collects 65% taxes but states bear 60%+ health expenditure; (2) Conditional grants reduce fiscal autonomy; (3) Smaller states — capacity constraints in meeting conditionalities; (4) NHM grants (separate from FC grants): 60:40 Centre:State ratio — matching requirement challenges poorer states. Impact: (1) Local body health functions strengthened; (2) Urban primary healthcare (ward-level HWCs); (3) State accountability through conditional framework. Critique: Amount inadequate; conditionalities may exclude weakest states; overlap with NHM creates coordination burden.

question: भारत में 'Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 (Colonial)' की legacy और proposed Public Health Emergency Management Act को critically examine करें।

options.text: Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 — modern India में inapplicable है

EDA 1897: only 4 sections; vests extraordinary powers in state governments; colonial 'command and control' approach; invoked in COVID-19 2020; COVID amendment (2020) — healthcare worker protection (Section 2B); no rights-based framework, no compensation, no planning mandate; Public Health Emergency Management Act (proposed) — not enacted as of 2024
EDA 1897 — केवल central government को powers देता है
EDA 1897 को COVID-19 के दौरान invoke नहीं किया गया था

explanation: Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 — Colonial Legacy: Context: Written during Bombay Plague 1897; originally to give extraordinary powers to deal with cholera/plague. Only 4 sections. Key provisions: (1) Section 2: State governments may take 'special measures'; (2) Section 2A: Central government powers for ships/vessels; (3) Section 3: Penalty for disobedience; (4) Section 4: Immunity for good faith actions. Invoked during: SARS 2003, H1N1 2009, COVID-19 March 2020. COVID 2020 Amendment: Added Section 2B — protection for healthcare workers from violence (attacks on doctors/nurses during COVID). Limitations: (1) No rights-based framework; (2) No pandemic preparedness planning mandate; (3) No quarantine compensation; (4) No evidence-based response requirements; (5) No Centre-State coordination mechanism. Public Health Emergency Management Act (proposed): Based on IHR 2005; comprehensive — surveillance, response, compensation, quarantine rights, laboratory network. Status: Not enacted as of 2024. COVID lesson: Comprehensive public health law needed.

question: भारत में 'ICESCR Article 12' और India's obligations को General Comment 14 (AAAQ framework) के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: India ने ICESCR ratify नहीं किया है

India ratified ICESCR 1979; Art. 12 — right to highest attainable standard of health; CESCR General Comment 14 (2000): AAAQ framework (Availability, Accessibility, Acceptability, Quality); courts use ICESCR as interpretive aid (Vishaka principle); UPR reviews — OOPE, MMR, NHM gaps flagged; not directly justiciable without domestic legislation
ICESCR obligations — India में directly judicially enforceable हैं
General Comment 14 — ICESCR का formal amendment है

explanation: ICESCR Art. 12 and India: International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights: India ratified 1979. Art. 12: States recognize right of everyone to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health.
