Art. 12(2): Steps — reduction of stillbirth rate, infant mortality; healthy development of the child; improvement of environmental and industrial hygiene; prevention, treatment and control of epidemic diseases; creation of conditions to assure medical service. CESCR General Comment 14 (2000): AAAQ Framework: (1) Availability: sufficient quantity of functioning healthcare facilities; (2) Accessibility: physical + economic + information + non-discriminatory; (3) Acceptability: culturally appropriate, gender-sensitive; (4) Quality: medically and scientifically appropriate. India's UPR (Universal Periodic Review) — health gaps flagged: OOPE (48.2% of CHE), maternal mortality, NHM implementation. Judicial use: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997): International conventions used as interpretive aid; Indian courts use ICESCR to strengthen Art. 21 interpretation. Not directly justiciable: ICESCR not incorporated into domestic law by Parliament. HEO: AAAQ framework for health services planning.

question: भारत में 'NMC Act 2020' को MCI की failures और 'bridge course' controversy के संदर्भ में critically analyze करें।

options.text: NMC Act 2020 — Medical Council of India को strengthen करता है

NMC 2020: MCI abolished (regulatory capture, corruption, CBI raids); NMC = 33-member elected+nominated; NEXT (National Exit Test) — common licensing + PG entrance; Section 49 bridge course for AYUSH practitioners in Scheduled Areas — IMA called 'mixing of systems'; private medical college fee autonomy — concern
NEXT exam — केवल MBBS graduates के लिए है, PG के लिए नहीं
NMC Act 2020 में AYUSH practitioners का कोई mention नहीं है

explanation: NMC Act 2020 — Critical Analysis: MCI abolished: Medical Council of India (1956) — regulatory capture, corruption in college approvals; CBI raid on MCI officials. National Medical Commission (NMC) Act 2020: (1) NMC: 33 members; Sub-committees: UGMEB, PGMEB, Medical Assessment and Rating Board, Ethics and Medical Registration Board; (2) NEXT (National Exit Test): common licensing + PG entrance exam; (3) Common Counselling for PG admissions. Major controversies: (1) Bridge course: Section 49 — AYUSH practitioners can prescribe modern medicine after 3.5-year bridge course in Scheduled Areas; IMA called 'mixing of systems' — threatened strike; Parliamentary Committee recommended deletion; (2) Fee regulation weakened — private medical college fee autonomy; (3) Government nominations increase — reduces professional autonomy. Positive aspects: (1) NEXT — standardizes quality; (2) Common Counselling — reduces private college dominance; (3) Ethics Board — clearer grievance redressal. Status: NEXT exam being piloted; bridge course implementation pending/disputed.

question: भारत में 'One Health approach' को governance और legal framework के संदर्भ में critically examine करें — animal-human-environment interface, Nipah, COVID।

options.text: One Health — India में formally adopted है with integrated legal framework

One Health: human-animal-environment interface; India lacks integrated legal framework — MoHFW (human), DAHD (animal), MoEFCC (environment) — siloed; IDSP + NVBDCP + PVO Act + Environment Acts = fragmented; Kerala Nipah (2018) — successful integrated response; PM-ABHIM — One Health platform proposed but not enacted
IDSP covers animal disease surveillance effectively
WHO One Health Joint Plan — India signatory नहीं है

explanation: One Health in India — Governance Analysis: One Health concept: human health, animal health, and ecosystem health are interconnected; requires integrated governance. India's governance landscape: (1) Human health: MoHFW; IDSP; (2) Animal health: Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying (DAHD); (3) Environment: MoEFCC; wildlife — WII. Legal frameworks (siloed): Prevention and Control of Infectious and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act 2009; Wildlife Protection Act 1972; Environment Protection Act 1986; Epidemic Diseases Act 1897. Nipah virus (Kerala 2018, 2021): Fruit bat (Pteropus) → human transmission; Kerala government integrated health, veterinary, forest departments — relatively successful. COVID-19: animal-origin pandemic; INSACOG (genome sequencing) — delayed activation. PM-ABHIM (2021): One Health platform proposed — integrate human + animal surveillance. WHO-FAO-UNEP One Health Joint Plan of Action (2022): India signatory. Challenges: (1) Departmental silos; (2) Veterinary human resource shortage; (3) No integrated zoonosis surveillance. HEO: One Health IEC — zoonosis prevention (rabies, brucellosis, avian influenza).

question: भारत में 'National Food Security Act 2013' का health outcomes पर critically examine करें — food entitlements, nutritional adequacy, और implementation gaps।

options.text: NFSA 2013 — malnutrition को completely eliminate करता है

NFSA 2013: 75% rural + 50% urban को subsidized grain (5 kg/person ₹1-3); maternity entitlement; ICDS meals; BUT caloric focus — micronutrient gap unaddressed; Aadhaar linkage exclusion errors; NFHS-5 stunting 35.5% — NFSA not solved malnutrition; ONORC portability; POSHAN Abhiyaan as complement
NFSA 2013 — केवल PDS grains को regulate करता है, MCH entitlements नहीं
NFSA 2013 — state governments को implement करने की obligation नहीं है

explanation: NFSA 2013 and Health: National Food Security Act 2013: (1) Priority households: 75% rural, 50% urban; 5 kg/person/month at ₹1 (millets), ₹2 (wheat), ₹3 (rice); (2) Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY): 35 kg/household at same price; (3) Maternity entitlement: ₹6,000 (partially implemented through PMMVY ₹5,000); (4) Meals for children 6 months-14 years (ICDS, MDM). Health-nutrition gap: (1) Caloric adequacy — somewhat addressed; (2) Micronutrient deficiency (iron, folic acid, Vitamin A, B12) — PDS doesn't address; (3) Stunting (NFHS-5): 35.5% — minimal improvement from 38.4% (NFHS-4); (4) Wasting: 19.3% (high); (5) Anaemia in women: 57%. Aadhaar linkage exclusion errors: legitimate poor excluded. ONORC (One Nation One Ration Card): portability for migrant workers — health implications. POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018): multi-ministerial convergence to address malnutrition beyond food security. HEO: NFSA awareness; nutrition counselling — caloric adequacy ≠ nutritional adequacy.

question: भारत में 'Occupational Health and Safety' को legal framework — Factories Act 1948, BOCW Act 1996, OSH Code 2020 — के संदर्भ में critically examine करें।

options.text: Occupational health — India में unregulated है

Factories Act 1948: manufacturing workers; BOCW Act 1996: construction workers (12 crore+) — cess fund ₹50,000+ crore accumulated but underutilized; OSH Code 2020: consolidated 13 labor laws; informal sector (94% workforce) = largely outside OSH framework; silicosis, asbestosis, pesticide poisoning — major burdens
OSH Code 2020 — agricultural workers को fully cover करता है
Factories Act 1948 — सभी workplaces पर apply होता है

explanation: Occupational Health Legal Framework: Factories Act 1948: Manufacturing facilities with 10+ workers (power); occupational health provisions — medical examinations, first aid, canteen, rest rooms, health officers in large factories. BOCW (Building and Other Construction Workers) Act 1996: 12+ crore construction workers; welfare fund (1% cess on construction cost); benefits — accidental death, disability, maternity; but cess fund massively underutilized (₹50,000+ crore accumulated, poorly spent on welfare). OSH Code 2020: Consolidated 13 labor laws including Factories Act, Mines Act, BOCW; extended to contract workers, fixed-term employees. Coverage gaps: (1) Agricultural workers: NO OSH protection; (2) Informal sector (94%): largely outside; (3) Gig economy workers (Zomato, Ola): contested classification. Health hazards: Silicosis (stone quarrying — UP, Rajasthan), asbestosis, pesticide poisoning (agriculture), occupational cancer. ILO C187 (Promotional Framework for OSH) — India ratified 2021 — commitment to national OSH profile. HEO: occupational health in informal sector; silicosis camps in mining areas; pesticide safety awareness.

question: भारत में 'Environmental Justice और health rights' के बीच linkage को M.C. Mehta cases, NGT Act 2010, और Absolute Liability doctrine के संदर्भ में critically analyze करें।

options.text: Environmental protection — health rights से legally disconnect है

Art. 21 = right to clean environment (Subhash Kumar 1991); M.C. Mehta cases — Ganga/air pollution → health link; Absolute Liability (Oleum Gas 1986) — no exceptions for hazardous industry; NGT Act 2010 — specialized environmental justice; Precautionary Principle + Polluter Pays = health protective; 1.67 million deaths/year from air pollution
NGT — health complaints directly adjudicate करता है
Absolute Liability — केवल nuclear plants पर apply होती है

explanation: Environmental Justice and Health Rights: Constitutional foundation: Art. 48A: State shall endeavour to protect and improve environment; Art. 51A(g): Fundamental duty. Judicial expansion: Art. 21 = right to live in healthy environment: (1) Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991): right to pollution-free water and air = life under Art. 21; (2) M.C. Mehta v. Union of India — Ganga pollution, vehicular pollution Delhi (CNG order 2001); (3) M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997): Public Trust Doctrine; (4) Oleum Gas leak case (1986): Absolute Liability — no exceptions for hazardous industries (unlike Rylands v. Fletcher). NGT Act 2010: Specialized tribunal; health = explicit consideration; Original + Appellate jurisdiction; 5 benches. Key principles: Precautionary Principle + Polluter Pays (includes health damage compensation). Health burden: 1.67 million deaths/year from air pollution (State of Global Air 2023). Bhopal Gas Tragedy (1984) — led to Absolute Liability doctrine. HEO: Environment-health nexus in IEC; One Health approach.

question: भारत में 'Delegated Legislation in Health' को critically examine करें — Statutory Rules, Executive Orders, और Parliamentary oversight।

options.text: Health sector में कोई delegated legislation नहीं है

Delegated legislation in health: Rules under D&C Act (CDSCO rules), MTP Rules, PC-PNDT Rules, NMC Regulations — Parliament delegates rule-making to executive; scrutinized by Committee on Subordinate Legislation; 'Henry VIII clauses' (override parent act) — concern; EVPBA 2019 (e-cigarette ban) via ordinance; sub-ordinate legislation = critical for health governance
Statutory rules — Parliament की approval के बिना never operate करती हैं
Executive Orders — health में legal force नहीं रखते

explanation: Delegated Legislation in Health: Parliament passes broad enabling laws; delegates rule/regulation-making to executive. Health examples: (1) Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945 — under D&C Act; updated regularly by CDSCO; (2) MTP Rules 2003 — approved doctor qualifications, facility standards; (3) PC-PNDT Rules 1996 — registration, record-keeping for USG machines; (4) NMC Regulations — NEXT exam format, curriculum; (5) NDCT Rules 2019 — clinical trial conduct. Parliamentary scrutiny: Committee on Subordinate Legislation (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha) — reviews rules/regulations; recommends modification; but capacity limited. 'Henry VIII clauses': provisions allowing executive to modify parent Act through rules — constitutionally suspect. EVPBA 2019: e-cigarette ban via executive ordinance — questioned for lack of legislative backing. MHA 2017: allows government to prescribe procedures beyond Act's mandate — concern. HEO: must follow delegated legislation (MTP Rules, PC-PNDT Rules) as binding law; rules change frequently — staying updated is compliance obligation.

question: भारत में 'HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act 2017' को anti-discrimination और treatment rights के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: India में HIV/AIDS को regulate करने वाला कोई law नहीं है

HIV AIDS Act 2017: first dedicated legislation; prohibits discrimination in employment, healthcare, education; ombudsman mechanism; informed consent for testing mandatory; confidentiality; PLHIV rights-based approach; BUT implementation — ombudsman rarely functional; stigma in healthcare facilities persists
HIV AIDS Act 2017 — केवल PLHIV को ART free देने का mandate है
HIV testing — India में mandatory है सभी के लिए

explanation: HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act 2017: First dedicated legislation for HIV in India. Key provisions: (1) Prohibition of discrimination: Section 3 — no discrimination in employment, healthcare, education, property, housing, insurance; (2) Informed consent: mandatory for HIV testing; cannot be tested without consent except court order; (3) Confidentiality: Section 34 — identity of HIV+ person protected; disclosure = penal offence; (4) Ombudsman: State-level complaints mechanism; (5) Rights of PLHIV (People Living with HIV): access to ART (though free ART = pre-existing policy, not new legal right); (6) Guardianship of HIV+ orphans. NACP (National AIDS Control Programme): Phase I (1992) to Phase V (2021-26) — ART centers, ICTC (Integrated Counseling and Testing Centers), prevention programs. Implementation gaps: (1) Ombudsman not functional in most states; (2) Healthcare workers still refuse PLHIV treatment (discrimination); (3) Stigma in facility delivery for HIV+ women; (4) Insurance exclusion of HIV — Act says discrimination prohibited but industry practice varies. HEO: PLHIV rights IEC; destigmatization; mandatory reporting of discrimination.

question: भारत में 'Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019' के healthcare provisions को critically evaluate करें — NALSA judgment 2014 और implementation gap।

options.text: Transgender Persons Act 2019 — healthcare को directly address नहीं करता

NALSA v. Union of India (2014): transgender = third gender; fundamental rights (Art. 14, 15, 19, 21); Transgender Persons Act 2019: Section 15 — government to provide healthcare; National Council for Transgender Persons; BUT self-certification of gender = long process; healthcare facilities non-inclusive; mental health pathologization critique
NALSA judgment — Parliament द्वारा overruled किया गया था
Transgender Persons Act 2019 — criminal penalties for discrimination शामिल नहीं करता

explanation: Transgender Health Rights: NALSA v. Union of India (2014): 9-judge bench; transgender persons = 'third gender'; Fundamental Rights under Art. 14 (equality), 15 (non-discrimination), 19 (expression), 21 (dignity, life); directed government to take steps for their welfare including healthcare. Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019: (1) Self-identification of gender (with some process requirements — criticized as cumbersome); (2) Section 15: Government must provide healthcare facilities — separate HIV surveillance, sex reassignment surgery, comprehensive medical insurance; (3) Section 11: Designation of Designated Officers; (4) National Council for Transgender Persons. Implementation gaps: (1) Healthcare facilities non-inclusive — refusal of care, discrimination documented; (2) Sex reassignment surgery: few government hospitals offer; (3) Mental health: WHO removed gender dysphoria from ICD-11 mental disorders → India's MHA 2017 doesn't address this; (4) Screening: transgender persons excluded from routine MCH screening programs; (5) Certificate process for gender identity — complex, discourages use. Civil society critique: Act weakened NALSA protections. UNHCR and international bodies: concerned about India's implementation. HEO: transgender-inclusive health services; non-discriminatory IEC.

question: भारत में 'Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005' का health implications के संदर्भ में critically examine करें — PWDVA और medical evidence।

options.text: PWDVA 2005 — healthcare workers की कोई role नहीं है

PWDVA 2005: civil law protection; shelter homes, protection orders, residence rights; health implications — IPV causes injury, mental health, reproductive coercion, miscarriage; healthcare workers = mandatory reporters in some state guidelines; MLC (Medico-Legal Certificate) critical; IMR-violence nexus; HEO: IPV screening in MCH
PWDVA 2005 — criminal punishment देता है domestic violence के लिए
Medical evidence — PWDVA cases में inadmissible है

explanation: PWDVA 2005 and Health: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005: Civil law (criminal = IPC Section 498A — cruelty by husband/relatives). PWDVA provisions: (1) Domestic violence: physical, sexual, verbal/emotional, economic; (2) Protection Orders: prevents abuser from contacting victim; (3) Residence Orders: victim cannot be evicted; (4) Shelter homes; (5) Protection Officers; (6) Medical Officers: can be asked to examine victim and issue certificate. Health implications of IPV (Intimate Partner Violence): (1) Physical injury — fractures, burns, TBI (Traumatic Brain Injury); (2) Mental health — depression, PTSD, suicidal ideation; (3) Reproductive health — forced sex → STIs, unwanted pregnancy, unsafe abortion, miscarriage; (4) Child health — IPV household → malnutrition, stunting, childhood trauma; (5) Femicide risk. NFHS-5: 29.3% women (18-49) experienced physical/sexual violence from husband. Healthcare workers' role: (1) Medico-Legal Certificate (MLC): legal documentation; (2) Mandatory reporting — no universal legal requirement in India (unlike some states' protocols); (3) ASHAs: trained to identify and refer IPV cases. HEO: IPV screening in antenatal care; safe referral pathways; 181 helpline awareness.

question: भारत में 'POCSO Act 2012 (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences)' के mandatory reporting provisions को healthcare workers' obligation के संदर्भ में critically examine करें।

options.text: POCSO Act 2012 — healthcare workers पर कोई mandatory reporting obligation नहीं डालता

POCSO Section 19: mandatory reporting by ANY person including healthcare workers — failure = 6 months imprisonment; child-friendly medical examination; SJPU (Special Juvenile Police Unit) coordination; BUT: mandatory reporting vs. therapeutic relationship tension; reporting by HEO = legal obligation
POCSO — केवल schools में applicable है
POCSO Act — 18 वर्ष से कम के perpetrators पर apply नहीं होता

explanation: POCSO Act 2012 and Healthcare Workers: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012: Comprehensive child sexual abuse legislation. Child-friendly features: (1) Child-friendly statements — not re-victimization; (2) Medical examination by female doctor only for girl victim; (3) Examination within 24 hours of report; (4) SJPU involvement. Mandatory Reporting (Section 19): ANY person who has knowledge of POCSO offence MUST report to SJPU or police; includes healthcare workers (doctors, nurses, HEOs, ASHAs). Failure to report = punishable with 6 months imprisonment + fine. Child → healthcare: (1) Presentation with STI in child < 18 = mandatory reporting; (2) Unexplained injuries; (3) Behavioral changes + physical signs; (4) Pregnancy in minor. Tensions: (1) Mandatory reporting vs. therapeutic confidentiality; (2) Fear of family-child separation; (3) Re-traumatization risk if not handled properly; (4) Healthcare provider reluctance. Child care institutions: POCSO extends to children in care homes, juvenile homes. Amendment 2019: Death penalty for aggravated offences (child < 16); enhanced minimum sentences. HEO: mandatory training on POCSO; must report; also IEC for parents and community.

question: भारत में 'Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016' को health और environmental safety के संदर्भ में critically analyze करें।

options.text: Bio-Medical Waste Management — केवल large hospitals को concern करता है

BMWM Rules 2016 (updated 2018, 2019): 4-color coded waste segregation; Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities (CBWTF); all HCFs (including private clinics) obligated; COVID surge exposed gaps; needle-stick injuries — occupational risk; compliance: urban > rural; CPCB oversight; HEO: BMW IEC in health facilities
BMWM Rules 2016 — CPCB के jurisdiction में नहीं है
Private clinics — BMWM Rules 2016 से exempt हैं

explanation: Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016 and Health: BMWM Rules 2016 (under Environment Protection Act 1986): Replaced BMW Rules 1998. Key provisions: (1) All healthcare facilities (HCF) — government + private, including clinics — must comply; (2) 4-color coded waste segregation: Yellow (anatomical, soiled), Red (contaminated recyclables), White (sharps), Blue (glassware); (3) Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities (CBWTF) — districts must have; (4) Autoclaving, incineration, deep burial — specific requirements; (5) Accident reporting; (6) Staff training mandatory. Health risks of improper BMW: (1) Needle-stick injuries → HIV, Hepatitis B/C transmission (occupational); (2) Rag-pickers sorting hospital waste → infection; (3) Illegal reuse of syringes; (4) Groundwater contamination. COVID-19 BMW surge: PPE kits, masks, syringes — massive increase; CPCB guidelines on COVID BMW; small clinics overwhelmed. Compliance gaps: (1) Rural private clinics — low compliance; (2) CBWTF not in all districts; (3) Training inadequate. CPCB oversight: Annual compliance reports; state PCBs enforce. Amendments 2018, 2019: Mercury thermometers phase-out; new categories. HEO: BMW segregation IEC in health facilities; occupational safety — needle-stick protocols.

question: भारत में 'Medical Device Regulation' की evolution को critically examine करें — D&C Act से Medical Devices Rules 2017/2020 तक।

options.text: Medical devices — India में unregulated हैं

Medical Devices Rules 2017/2020 (under D&C Act): CDSCO regulation; class A-D risk classification; mandatory clinical investigation for high-risk; in vitro diagnostics (IVD) included; import regulation; BUT: Post-Market Surveillance weak; 'spurious devices' issue; stent/knee implant price control (NPPA) — patient access vs innovation tension
Medical devices — केवल pharmaceutical drugs के साथ regulate होते हैं
NPPA — medical device prices regulate नहीं करती

explanation: Medical Device Regulation in India: Historical context: Medical devices regulated under Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 — inadequate. Medical Devices Rules 2017 (effective 2018, amended 2020): (1) All medical devices now under regulation (phased approach); (2) Risk classification: Class A (low risk) to Class D (high risk — pacemakers, stents, implants); (3) Manufacturing license; (4) Import regulation: registration + clinical data; (5) In Vitro Diagnostics (IVD): COVID test kits — pandemic relevance; (6) Clinical investigation requirement for Class C/D. NPPA price regulation: Stents (coronary) — price capped 2017 (₹29,600 from ₹1.5 lakh); knee implants — price capped; Essential Medical Devices Order (EMDO) concept. Regulatory gaps: (1) Post-Market Surveillance weak — no mandatory reporting of device failures (unlike USA FDA MedWatch); (2) 'Spurious devices' in market; (3) AI-based devices (diagnostic AI) — regulatory framework being developed; (4) Ayurvedic devices — jurisdiction unclear. Innovation-access tension: Price caps discourage investment; but patient access improved. CDSCO: Single National Regulatory Authority (medical devices + drugs) — resources stretched. HEO: Medical device quality in health facilities; reporting of device failures.

question: 'National Disaster Management Act 2005' और health emergencies के बीच intersection को critically analyze करें — NDMA, NDRF, और COVID governance।

options.text: NDMA Act 2005 — health emergencies को specifically cover नहीं करता

DM Act 2005: NDMA (PM chairs) — disaster management; health emergency ≠ explicitly defined 'disaster'; COVID 2020 — lockdowns under DM Act (Section 6); NDRF deployment for disaster health; SDMA at state level; DM Act + EDA 1897 + essential services = COVID legal basis; constitutional challenge to lockdown orders
NDMA — Ministry of Health के under है
DM Act 2005 — Centre को state health systems को directly takeover करने का power देता है

explanation: Disaster Management Act 2005 and Health: DM Act 2005: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) — PM as Chair; National Executive Committee (NEC) — Cabinet Secretary; State Disaster Management Authorities (SDMA) — CM as Chair; District DMA — Collector. Legal powers: (1) NDMA: lay down policies, plans and guidelines; (2) NEC: coordinate and monitor implementation; (3) Section 6(2)(i): NDMA can direct any ministry/department. COVID-19 legal basis: (1) DM Act Section 6 — NDMA issued National Directives for COVID management (lockdown, containment); (2) Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 — states used for quarantine, section orders; (3) Essential Services Maintenance Act — health services declared essential. Lockdown constitutionality: (1) High Court PILs challenged lockdown orders — courts largely upheld citing public health emergency; (2) Art. 19 restrictions (movement, assembly) — 'reasonable restriction' in public interest justified; (3) No formal Emergency (Art. 352) declared. SDMA's COVID role: State quarantine centers, enforcement of containment zones, coordination with district administration. DM Act gaps for health: (1) 'Biological disaster' — definition ambiguous; (2) No mandatory health preparedness plan; (3) Proposed: Public Health Emergency of National Concern (PHENC) designation. HEO: ICS (Incident Command System) in health emergencies.

question: भारत में 'NDPS Act 1985 (Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances)' को harm reduction approach और public health के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: NDPS Act 1985 — harm reduction को explicitly support करता है

NDPS Act 1985: criminal approach (possession = 6 months to 20 years); personal use vs. trafficking distinction — limited; harm reduction (needle exchange, OST) = parallel public health policy not integrated in NDPS; Section 2 definition of 'small quantity' — scientific basis contested; PWUD criminalization increases HIV/HCV risk
NDPS Act 1985 — health approach को prioritize करता है punishment से over
Harm reduction programs — NDPS Act के under illegal हैं India में

explanation: NDPS Act 1985 and Public Health: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act 1985: Criminal framework — focus on supply reduction. Key provisions: (1) Personal consumption: 'small quantity' = 6 months-1 year; 'intermediate quantity' = up to 10 years; 'commercial quantity' = up to 20 years (minimum 10 years); (2) Bail provisions: stringent for commercial quantity (reverse burden of proof); (3) NDPS Act Amendment 2014: some provisions relaxed for medical use (opiates for palliative care). Harm Reduction (public health approach): (1) Needle Syringe Programme (NSP) — clean needles to PWID (People Who Inject Drugs); prevents HIV, HCV, HBV; NACO-supported; (2) Opioid Substitution Therapy (OST) — Buprenorphine/Methadone; NACO + state government; legally permitted as medical treatment; (3) NACP provisions — but NDPS Act creates legal uncertainty. 'Small quantity' definition: Contested — 100mg heroin = small quantity in some states; scientific basis weak. Criminalization and health: (1) PWUD fear arrest → avoid testing/treatment; (2) HIV among PWID in Manipur, Nagaland — high burden; (3) Needle sharing → HIV clusters. Reform advocacy: Treat drug dependence as health condition (WHO recommendation) — India partially moving but NDPS framework = criminal. UNODC, WHO guidelines favor public health approach. HEO: awareness of harm reduction; non-judgmental approach to PWUD.

question: भारत में 'Inter-State Migrant Workers' की health rights को 'ISMW Act 1979' और 'OSH Code 2020' के संदर्भ में critically examine करें।

options.text: Inter-state migrant workers — किसी health scheme में covered नहीं हैं

ISMW Act 1979: contractor-mediated migrants (formal); benefits include medical facilities; but 90%+ migrants = informal sector; COVID 2020 — 10 crore migrant distress exposed governance gap; OSH Code 2020: portability provisions; ONORC — food security; e-Shram portal — registration; ESIC portability = major gap
ISMW Act 1979 — all migrant workers को cover करता है regardless of sector
COVID 2020 — migrant worker health crisis में State governments के पास कोई authority नहीं था

explanation: Inter-State Migrant Workers' Health Rights: Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979: Covers migrants employed through contractors; employers must provide medical facilities; displacement allowance. Coverage gap: Only formal sector contractor-mediated migrants — 90%+ migrants are informal (construction, brick kilns, domestic work) → NOT covered. COVID-19 crisis (March-May 2020): ~10 crore internal migrants; 'reverse migration' on foot; no food, shelter; health crisis — exhaustion, accidents, starvation deaths. Governance gap exposed: (1) No migrant worker registry; (2) Ration card not portable (partially addressed by ONORC); (3) ESIC not portable across states; (4) Destination state had welfare responsibility but origin state had migrant data. Post-COVID reform: (1) e-Shram portal (2021): voluntary registration of unorganized workers including migrants — ~28 crore registered; (2) ONORC (One Nation One Ration Card): food security portability; (3) OSH Code 2020: portability provisions for social security. Health programs: (1) ESIS portability: ESIC medical care should be portable across states — partially implemented; (2) PM-JAY: portable — works in any empanelled hospital. Remaining gaps: (1) Mental health of migrants (separation anxiety, poor conditions); (2) Occupational health in destination cities; (3) Child health — children of migrant workers left behind. HEO: migrant health outreach; ONORC awareness.

question: भारत में 'Genome India Project' और genomic data governance को privacy और ethics के संदर्भ में critically examine करें।

options.text: Genome India Project — केवल academic research है, governance issues नहीं हैं

Genome India Project (2020, ₹238 crore, DBT): 10,000 Indian genomes; diverse population diversity mapping; benefits — precision medicine; risks — population-level discrimination (insurer genetic profiling), biopiracy, data sovereignty; Puttaswamy privacy applies; no specific Genomic Data Protection law; DPDP Act 2023 — limited coverage
Genome India data — Aadhaar के साथ automatically linked है
Genomic data — personal data नहीं है under Puttaswamy

explanation: Genome India Project — Governance Analysis: Genome India Project (GIP) 2020: Department of Biotechnology (DBT) led; Budget: ₹238 crore; Objectives: (1) Sequence 10,000 Indian genomes (whole genome sequencing); (2) Map genetic diversity of India's 4,000+ communities; (3) Create reference dataset for precision medicine, disease prediction, drug response. Benefits: (1) Precision medicine tailored to Indian population; (2) Understanding population-specific disease risks (pharmacogenomics); (3) Drug discovery. Governance and Ethics concerns: (1) Consent: individual informed consent vs. population-level implications — tribal communities' collective consent; (2) Data sovereignty: where stored? (National Biological Data Centre, Faridabad); (3) Insurance discrimination: genetic information used to deny/price insurance — no specific genomic non-discrimination law in India; (4) Biopiracy concern: foreign researchers accessing Indian data; (5) Commercial exploitation: benefit sharing with communities? Legal framework: Puttaswamy (2017): genetic data = sensitive personal information = privacy right. DPDP Act 2023: 'sensitive personal data' — but genetic data governance inadequate. International: UNESCO Declaration on Human Genome and Human Rights (1997) — India signatory. Biological Diversity Act 2002: benefit-sharing for biological resources (adjacent to genomics). HEO relevance: genomic medicine in future health systems; ethical IEC.

question: भारत में 'National Blood Policy' और Blood Transfusion safety को critically examine करें — Voluntary Blood Donation, NBTC, और paid blood donation risks।

options.text: Blood transfusion — India में fully safe और regulated है

National Blood Policy 2002: 100% voluntary non-remunerated blood donation (VNRBD) target; NBTC (National Blood Transfusion Council); paid donation = illegal but persists; NAT (Nucleic Acid Testing) for HIV/HCV — not universal in all blood banks; rational transfusion practices — gap; Transfusion Transmitted Infections (TTI) risk
Paid blood donation — India में fully legal है
NBTC — state blood transfusion councils को directly control करती है

explanation: Blood Transfusion Safety and Governance: National Blood Policy 2002: (1) 100% Voluntary Non-Remunerated Blood Donation (VNRBD) target; (2) NBTC (National Blood Transfusion Council): apex body, policy formulation; (3) State Blood Transfusion Councils (SBTC): state level coordination. Legal framework: Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 (Schedule F Part X) + Blood Bank Regulations 1999: (1) Blood banks must be licensed by state drug controller; (2) Paid blood donation — prohibited; (3) NAT (Nucleic Acid Testing) — recommended for HIV, HCV, HBV; not mandatory in all blood banks; (4) Hemovigilance: NBTC launched National Haemovigilance Programme (NHP) — adverse transfusion reaction reporting. Reality: (1) VNRBD target not achieved — ~70% voluntary; (2) Professional/replacement donors persist in some states; (3) NAT not available in all blood banks — HIV window period risk; (4) Rational transfusion practices (avoid unnecessary transfusions) — not universally followed; (5) Anemia → repeated transfusion → TTI risk (especially in thalassemia, sickle cell). WHO recommendation: 100% VNRBD achievable with awareness campaigns. HEO: blood donation IEC; World Blood Donor Day (June 14) campaigns; community drives.

question: भारत में 'Health Impact Assessment (HIA)' की concept को regulatory requirement के रूप में critically examine करें — EIA और HIA integration।

options.text: Health Impact Assessment — India में mandatory है सभी projects के लिए

HIA — India में not mandatory; Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) 2006 — limited health chapter; EIA Notification 2020 Draft — health provisions weakened; WHO HIA promotes for all policies; SEHA (Strategic Environmental and Health Assessment) concept; MoHFW + MoEFCC coordination gap; industry resistance to HIA mandate
EIA और HIA — India में same instrument हैं
HIA — केवल pharmaceutical projects के लिए India में required है

explanation: Health Impact Assessment in India — Governance Analysis: Health Impact Assessment (HIA): Systematic process to evaluate potential health effects of proposed policy/project/program. International: WHO defines HIA; essential for Health in All Policies (HiAP). India's EIA system: EIA (Environmental Impact Assessment) Notification 2006 — under Environment Protection Act 1986; required for specified industries, infrastructure. Health in EIA: (1) Health chapter mandatory in EIA report — baseline health, impact assessment; (2) But health chapter often superficial — data quality poor; (3) No mandatory HIA separate from EIA; (4) No dedicated HIA authority. EIA Notification 2020 Draft: Proposed to weaken EIA including health provisions — public protest, withdrawn partially. Industry resistance: HIA seen as additional burden, project delay. Examples where HIA needed: (1) Coal thermal plants — air pollution health impact; (2) Mining in tribal areas — occupational + community health; (3) Highway construction — accident risk; (4) FMCG factories — chemical exposure. WHO HiAP (Health in All Policies): Government India endorsed at WHO — but implementation absent. Positive examples: Some state-level industrial health impact studies. HEO: advocate for HIA in local industrial projects; document community health baseline.

question: भारत में 'National Policy for Children 2013' को child health rights और CRC obligations के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: India ने UN Convention on Rights of the Child (CRC) ratify नहीं किया है

India ratified CRC 1992; National Policy for Children 2013: 4 priority areas — survival, health, nutrition, development; 18 years = child; BUT: NPC 2013 = policy not law; child health programs (ICDS, MAA, JSSK) — implementation gaps; POCSO, JJ Act = stronger legal force; child budget = declining share
National Policy for Children 2013 — law है जिसे enforce किया जा सकता है
CRC obligations — India में domestic law में incorporated हैं

explanation: National Policy for Children 2013 and CRC: UN Convention on Rights of the Child (CRC): India ratified November 1992. CRC rights relevant to health: (1) Art. 24: Right to the highest attainable standard of health; (2) Art. 25: Medical review for children in care; (3) Art. 26: Social security; (4) Art. 27: Adequate standard of living (nutrition). National Policy for Children 2013: (1) First comprehensive child policy since 1974; (2) 4 priority areas: Survival and Health; Education; Protection; Participation; (3) Defines child as below 18 years; (4) Calls for convergence of ICDS, NRHM, RMNCH+A. Health provisions: JSSK (Zero cost delivery for institutional birth), MAA (Mothers' Absolute Affection — breastfeeding promotion), free immunization (UIP), ICDS (nutrition), WIFS (Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation). NPC 2013 limitations: (1) Policy not law — no legal enforceability; (2) No dedicated monitoring mechanism; (3) Child budget (budget for children) = declining share of total budget. Stronger legal instruments: POCSO 2012, JJ Act 2015 (Juvenile Justice), Child Labor (Prohibition) Act 1986/2016, RTE Act 2009. HEO: child health rights; routine immunization; nutrition screening (MAM/SAM).

question: भारत में 'Water Quality and Public Health' को 'Jal Jeevan Mission', water quality standards, और legal framework के संदर्भ में critically analyze करें।

options.text: Jal Jeevan Mission — water quality को guarantee करता है सभी connections के लिए

JJM (2019, ₹3.6 lakh crore): functional household tap connections; water quality monitoring — field test kits (FTKs), accredited labs; BIS/WHO standards; BUT: quality vs. quantity tension; arsenic/fluoride contaminated water in some states; 'functional' vs. 'potable' connection gap; health-water-sanitation linkage
Water quality — India में केवल BIS के under regulate है, no public health law
JJM में water quality monitoring की कोई provision नहीं है

explanation: Water Quality and Public Health: Jal Jeevan Mission (2019): Har Ghar Jal — functional household tap connections to every rural household by 2024; Budget: ₹3.6 lakh crore; Progress: ~80%+ households covered (as of 2024). Water quality framework: (1) BIS IS 10500: Indian Standard for Drinking Water; (2) WHO Guidelines for Drinking Water Quality; (3) JJM water quality monitoring: Field Test Kits (FTK) at village level; Water Quality Monitoring and Surveillance (WQMS) by accredited labs; (4) Every Gram Panchayat must test water regularly. Quality challenges: (1) Arsenic contamination: 59+ districts in 21 states — West Bengal, Bihar, UP, Assam worst; (2) Fluoride: Rajasthan, Telangana, AP — dental/skeletal fluorosis; (3) Nitrate: agricultural runoff — infant methemoglobinemia; (4) Iron, TDS, hardness issues. Functional vs. Potable gap: JJM counts 'functional' connections (tap with water); but water may not be potable. Health-Water-Sanitation linkage: Diarrheal diseases — leading cause of child mortality; cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A — waterborne. SBM (Swachh Bharat Mission) + JJM together = WASH (Water, Sanitation, Hygiene). Right to safe drinking water: Art. 21 extension — Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar. HEO: water quality testing at village level; waterborne disease surveillance.

question: भारत में 'NITI Aayog Health Index' को federalism और competitive performance measurement के संदर्भ में critically evaluate करें।

options.text: NITI Aayog Health Index — states को binding targets देता है

NITI Aayog Health Index (2017, World Bank-assisted): 24 indicators; annual ranking of states; healthy competition; NHM funding linked to performance for 'aspirational states'; Kerala consistently tops; UP/Uttarakhand = incremental category; BUT: data quality issues; rank-gaming; smaller states advantage; doesn't capture out-of-pocket expenditure adequately
Health Index — Planning Commission ने develop किया था
Health Index rankings — states के NHM funding पर कोई impact नहीं होता

explanation: NITI Aayog Health Index — Critical Analysis: Launched 2017; World Bank technical assistance; Annual (5 iterations as of 2024). 24 indicators across 3 domains: (1) Health Outcomes: NMR, U5MR, IMR, MMR, full immunization; (2) Governance and Information: HMIS completeness, financial management; (3) Key Inputs/Processes: facility availability, healthcare providers, ANM/ASHA availability. Performance categories: (1) Large states; (2) Small states; (3) UTs; (4) Aspirational states (8 low-performing). Performance-incentive link: Aspirational states' NHM performance-based funds linked to index improvement. Competitive federalism tool: 'Cooperative and Competitive Federalism' — NITI Aayog philosophy. Top performers: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, AP consistently high. Low performers: UP, Uttarakhand, Bihar. Critical analysis: (1) Data quality: HMIS data quality variable — states with better reporting look better; (2) Rank-gaming: states improve reporting without improving services; (3) Composite indicators: loss of nuance; (4) OOPE (Out-Of-Pocket Expenditure): not adequately captured; (5) Smaller states advantage in some indicators; (6) Does not capture equity within states; (7) Gender dimensions limited. HEO contribution: accurate HMIS data improves state ranking — incentive for data quality.

question: भारत में 'Universal Immunization Programme (UIP)' की governance और liability framework को critically examine करें।

options.text: UIP — सभी children को vaccination देना voluntary है

UIP (1985, EPI 1978): 12 vaccines (pentavalent, IPV, rotavirus, PCV, MR, etc.); government obligation under Art. 21 and ICESCR; AEFI (Adverse Events Following Immunization) — reporting + compensation mechanism; Mission Indradhanush 2014 — intensification; state-level variations; HMIS coverage data vs. NFHS — gap
India में vaccination के लिए mandatory law है
AEFI compensation — India में legally mandated नहीं है

explanation: Universal Immunization Programme — Governance Analysis: UIP (1985, expanded from EPI 1978): Universal free immunization. Current vaccine schedule (12 vaccines): BCG, OPV, Hepatitis B, DPT, IPV, Pentavalent (DPT+Hib+HepB), PCV (pneumococcal), Rotavirus vaccine, MR, Japanese Encephalitis (in endemic areas), DPT booster, TT. New additions: Adult DT (2021), Typhoid Conjugate Vaccine (selected states). Legal basis: Not mandatory in law (no vaccination law in India — unlike some countries); but government obligation under Art. 21 read with ICESCR Art. 12. AEFI (Adverse Events Following Immunization): National AEFI Surveillance system; AEFI Secretariat at ITSU; Causality assessment; Compensation: No statutory compensation law — WHO recommendation; India has state-level ex-gratia payment; judicial decisions have ordered compensation. Mission Indradhanush (2014): Intensification for missed/under-immunized children; Phase I-V; Intensified MI (2017), IMI (2019). Coverage gap: Government claims 90%+; NFHS-5 full immunization: 76.4% (12-23 months) — significant gap from official claims; rural-urban, caste-class disparities. HEO: microplan for immunization sessions; AEFI reporting; missed children tracking.

question: भारत में 'Transformative Constitutionalism' का health rights पर critically examine करें — B.R. Ambedkar vision, Navtej Johar, और Section 377 decriminalization के health implications।

options.text: Transformative Constitutionalism — health rights से unrelated concept है

Transformative Constitutionalism (Karl Klare): Constitution as instrument of societal transformation; Ambedkar — Constitution for social revolution; Navtej Johar v. Union of India (2018): Section 377 IPC decriminalized — MSM health impact (HIV prevention, mental health, healthcare access); constitutional morality > social morality
Navtej Johar — health rights को specifically discuss नहीं करता
Section 377 decriminalization — MSM community की health access पर कोई impact नहीं पड़ा

explanation: Transformative Constitutionalism and Health: Karl Klare's concept: Constitution as instrument for radical social transformation — courts as agents of change. B.R. Ambedkar: Constitution as mechanism for social revolution; abolition of untouchability (Art. 17), equality provisions = transformative health rights for Dalits/marginalized. Navtej Johar v. Union of India (2018): SC 5-judge bench — Section 377 IPC (carnal intercourse against the order of nature) decriminalized for consensual adult private acts. Health implications of 377 criminalization: (1) MSM (Men who have Sex with Men) fear reporting STIs/HIV; (2) Healthcare workers discriminate; (3) Mental health stigma = depression, suicide risk; (4) NACO MSM programs — undermined by criminalization; UNAIDS: criminalization = higher HIV risk. Post-Navtej Johar: (1) MSM can access healthcare without fear of prosecution; (2) LGBTQ+ health programs more open; (3) Mental health destigmatization. Constitutional Morality concept (D.Y. Chandrachud J.): Constitutional morality must prevail over social morality — rights don't depend on majoritarian acceptance. Transformative health rights: Art. 21 = right to live as whom you are. Supriyo v. Union of India (2023): No fundamental right to same-sex marriage — but health rights of LGBTQ+ = ongoing evolving area.

question: भारत में 'Directive Principles of State Policy (Art. 36-51)' और health के relationship को critically examine करें — Art. 39, 41, 42, 43, 47 के provisions।

options.text: DPSPs — health rights को explicitly mention नहीं करते

DPSPs health-relevant: Art. 39(e/f) — protect workers' health, children; Art. 41 — right to work, education, public assistance in sickness/disability; Art. 42 — just and humane conditions of work, maternity relief; Art. 43 — living wage; Art. 47 — raise nutrition levels, improve public health, prohibition (alcohol). DPSPs + Art. 21 = justiciable health obligations
DPSPs — courts द्वारा enforce नहीं किए जा सकते, इसलिए health पर कोई legal impact नहीं
Art. 47 — केवल nutrition को address करता है, health को नहीं

explanation: DPSPs and Health Rights — Critical Analysis: Directive Principles of State Policy (Art. 36-51): Not justiciable per se (Art. 37) but 'fundamental to governance' and must be applied in making laws. Health-relevant DPSPs: (1) Art. 39(e): State shall direct its policy — health/strength of workers (men, women, children) not abused; (2) Art. 39(f): Children given opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner; (3) Art. 41: Right to work, education, and public assistance in cases of sickness, disability, old age; (4) Art. 42: Provision for just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief; (5) Art. 43: Living wage + conditions of work ensuring decent standard of life; (6) Art. 47: State to raise nutrition level, standard of living, improvement of public health (primary responsibility) + endeavour to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health. SC jurisprudence: DPSPs must be read with Fundamental Rights; Art. 47 + Art. 21 = state's obligation to provide healthcare; Consumer Education case used Art. 47. Minnerva Mills (1980): Balance between FRs and DPSPs essential. HEO: DPSPs guide state health policy — NHP 2017, NLEM, free medicine, maternity benefits (Art. 42) = DPSP implementation.

question: भारत में 'Right to Health in Urban Areas' को 'Urban Primary Healthcare' और '74th Amendment' के संदर्भ में critically examine करें।

options.text: Urban health — India में rural NHM के समान program है

74th Amendment: ULBs responsible for urban health (Schedule 12, Item 6); but devolution poor; NUHM (National Urban Health Mission, 2013) within NHM; Urban HWCs planned; slum health — NFHS-5 shows better coverage in slums vs. rural in some states; urban health inequality = slum vs. rich; private sector dominance in urban
74th Amendment — urban health को mandatory ULB function बनाता है
NUHM — NHM से completely separate scheme है

explanation: Urban Health Rights — Constitutional and Policy Analysis: 74th Constitutional Amendment (1992): Urban Local Bodies (municipalities) — Schedule 12: 18 functions including Item 6 'Public Health, Sanitation, Conservancy and Solid Waste Management'. BUT: devolution = discretionary; most states retain health functions at state level; ULBs have weak capacity. Urban Health Policy: NUHM (National Urban Health Mission) 2013: Sub-mission of NHM; targets urban slum population; Urban Health & Wellness Centres; Urban Primary Health Centres; Urban Community Health Centres. Urban health dynamics: (1) Rapid urbanization — 40%+ population urban by 2030; (2) Urban slum health: NFHS-5 paradox — in some indicators, slum dwellers do better than rural (better access to facilities) but worse than non-slum urban; (3) Private sector = 75%+ urban ambulatory care; (4) Urban OOPE higher; (5) NCDs predominant in urban — lifestyle diseases. Urban inequality: (1) Gated communities vs. slums — within-city health inequality; (2) Poor urban migrants — not captured in NFHS sampling. 15th FC health grants: specific allocation for urban local bodies' health functions. HEO in urban context: slum health IEC; NCD screening; link with ULB health centers.

question: भारत में 'Health Minister और Health Secretary' के बीच political-bureaucratic relationship को critically analyze करें — NPM (New Public Management) reforms और health governance।

options.text: Health Minister और Secretary — same authority रखते हैं

Health Minister: elected, politically accountable; Health Secretary: IAS, permanent bureaucracy, technical implementation; tension: political priorities vs. technical advice; NPM reforms — NHM Mission Director (specialist); ASHA incentive payment delays = bureaucratic-political blame-shifting; Mission Steering Group (MSG) = apex body chaired by Health Minister
Health Secretary — Minister की policies को veto कर सकता है
NHM Mission Director — Health Secretary के under होता है

explanation: Political-Bureaucratic Interface in Health: Health Ministry structure: (1) Union Health Minister: Cabinet rank; politically elected; accountable to Parliament; (2) Secretary (Health): IAS officer (usually); permanent bureaucracy; implements ministry decisions; (3) Secretary (Medical Research): ICMR oversight; (4) Director General of Health Services (DGHS): technical head — medical professional/IAS; (5) Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) Director General. State level: Minister + Secretary + Director (NHM Mission Director) + state DGHS. NHM governance innovation: Mission Steering Group (MSG): chaired by Minister; Mission Director (specialist) — separate from Secretary line. New Public Management (NPM) reforms in health: (1) NHM introduced 'Mission mode' with dedicated mission director — bypassing traditional bureaucratic hierarchy; (2) Performance-based incentives (RoP — Record of Proceedings); (3) Delegation to districts (District Health Society). Political-bureaucratic tension: (1) Political: populist health announcements (free dialysis, insurance expansion) without budget provision; (2) Bureaucratic: process compliance over outcomes; (3) ASHA incentive delays: state Health Secretary: 'funds not released'; Mission Director: 'PIPs not submitted'; Health Minister: 'all going well'; (4) COVID: clear command structure needed — often political messaging > technical advice. HEO operates under both political priorities and bureaucratic processes.

question: भारत में 'Health Sector Privatization' को 'Doctrine of State Action' और private hospitals' accountability के संदर्भ में critically examine करें।

options.text: Private hospitals — किसी constitutional obligation के under नहीं हैं

State Action doctrine: private entities performing 'public function' or 'substantially funded by state' = subject to FRs; Hospitals receiving government land, recognition, subsidies = potentially state action; Art. 12 (state) — SC inconsistently applied; Unnikrishnan (1993) applied to private education — health parallel; CEA 2010 = regulatory response
Unnikrishnan v. State of AP — medical education को regulate नहीं करता
Private hospitals — NHRC की jurisdiction में नहीं आते

explanation: State Action Doctrine and Private Hospitals: Art. 12: 'State' includes government + authorities controlled or substantially funded by government. Doctrinal development: (1) Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981): If government owns or substantially funds entity → 'State' under Art. 12; (2) Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993): Private educational institutions (though not state per se) must follow Art. 21 (right to education); regulatory framework justified — parallel argument for health; (3) T.M.A. Pai (2002): Private education autonomy — partial retreat from Unnikrishnan. Health application: (1) Private hospitals receiving government land at concessional rates, tax exemptions, government referrals — argument: they are quasi-state; (2) SC has not consistently applied Art. 12 to private hospitals; (3) No definitive SC ruling making private hospitals subject to FRs. Regulatory responses to accountability gap: (1) Clinical Establishments Act 2010 — state adoption (patchwork); (2) Consumer Protection Act — deficiency in service; (3) RTI — not applicable to most private hospitals; (4) NHRC: takes cases against private hospitals where state nexus proven; (5) State-specific private hospital regulations (Maharashtra, Delhi). PM-JAY: private empanelled hospitals = partially regulated through contract. HEO: navigates public-private partnership (PPP) hospitals where accountability structure is hybrid.

question: भारत में 'Community Health Workers (CHW) — ASHA' की legal status को critically examine करें — volunteer vs. employee, minimum wage, और labor rights।

options.text: ASHA — government employee हैं जिन्हें minimum wage मिलना चाहिए

ASHA = community volunteer (not employee per NHM guidelines); performance-based incentives, not salary; courts have NOT definitively ruled ASHA = employee; ASHA strikes (2019, 2022) demanding regularization; ESMA invocation threat by states; ILO C189 (Domestic Workers) — ASHA work analogous; Social protection gap = significant
ASHA को minimum wage — labor courts ने award किया है
ASHA — ESIC के under mandatory insured हैं

explanation: ASHA Legal Status — Critical Analysis: NHM framework: ASHA = 'community volunteer'; NOT government employee; receives 'performance-based incentives' (PBI) not salary. Incentive structure: (1) Fixed incentives: ~₹1,000-2,000/month (variable by state); (2) Variable: per JSY delivery, per immunization session, per RNTCP treatment completed — list of 60+ tasks; (3) Total ASHA earning: ₹3,000-8,000/month (varies hugely — rural vs. urban, state vs. state). Legal ambiguity: (1) 'Volunteer' = no ESI, no EPF, no minimum wage; (2) Courts: ASHAs approached labour courts — rulings inconsistent; some High Courts said they are not employees; (3) Social Security: NHM provides ASHA Group Accident Insurance (AGHI) — ₹2 lakh death; (4) COVID: ASHA worked as frontline workers — additional ₹1,000/month; COVID death — ₹25 lakh ex-gratia. ASHA strikes: 2019 (Delhi ASHA strike), 2022 (all-India demand) — regularization, minimum wage, social security; states threatened ESMA; union organizing by ASHA workers (ASHA workers under CITU, AITUC). ILO C189 (Domestic Workers Convention): India NOT ratified; but CHW work analogous to care work. HEO supervises ASHAs — must understand their legal status and vulnerability.

question: भारत में 'President's Rule (Art. 356)' और state health administration पर impact को critically examine करें — imposition और health programs continuity।

options.text: President's Rule — state health programs को automatically halt करता है

Art. 356: President's Rule = Governor administers state; Parliament exercises state legislature functions; health programs continue as bureaucracy-run (IAS); NHM PIPs can be modified; but political health policy decisions stalled; Bommai (1994) SC — restricted misuse; health continuity = administrative challenge
President's Rule में — Centre directly state hospitals को manage करता है
Bommai judgment — President's Rule को health emergencies में mandatory बनाता है

explanation: President's Rule and Health Administration: Art. 356: When state government cannot be carried on in accordance with Constitution; Governor reports → President proclaims President's Rule. Administration during President's Rule: (1) Governor administers the state; (2) Parliament assumes powers of state legislature; (3) Council of Ministers dissolved; (4) Bureaucracy (IAS) continues administration. Health program implications: (1) NHM continues: PIPs already approved — implementation proceeds; ASHA/ANM paid; (2) New political health policy decisions (free medicine expansion, new insurance scheme) = stalled — requires President/Governor approval; (3) State health budget: Parliament votes on state's demands for grants — opposition parties may object; (4) Emergency health decisions: Governor can take on ministerial advice of Centre. Bommai case (S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994): 9-judge bench — Art. 356 to be used sparingly; floor test before dismissal; courts can examine propriety; restricted misuse. Recent President's Rule (Uttarakhand 2016, Arunachal Pradesh 2016): health programs — temporary disruption then restored. Key principle: Health programs are executive in nature — continue; political health schemes = stalled. HEO: understands that health program implementation ≠ changes in political dispensation.

question: भारत में 'National Commission for Women (NCW)' और women's reproductive health rights enforcement को critically examine करें।

options.text: NCW — binding orders issue कर सकता है reproductive health violations के लिए

NCW (National Commission for Women Act 1990): quasi-judicial; investigates violations; reviews legislation affecting women; cases: sterilization deaths, sex selection, maternal mortality; recommendations non-binding; BUT: awareness + public pressure; state women's commissions variable capacity; CEDAW monitoring = international accountability layer
NCW — केवल domestic violence cases handle करता है
CEDAW — India में directly enforceable है domestic courts में

explanation: NCW and Women's Reproductive Health Rights: National Commission for Women (NCW) Act 1990: Statutory body; Chairperson + 5 members appointed by Central Government. Functions: (1) Review constitutional and legal safeguards for women; (2) Recommend remedial measures; (3) Take up cases of atrocities/violations; (4) Investigate specific complaints; (5) Reports to government. Reproductive health cases NCW has engaged with: (1) Sterilization camp deaths (Chhattisgarh 2014 — 15 deaths during mass sterilization camp); (2) Sex selection and female foeticide; (3) Maternal mortality in institutional delivery; (4) Child marriage and health consequences; (5) Forced hysterectomies in tribal women (Chhattisgarh, 2019). Limitations: (1) Recommendations non-binding — government may ignore; (2) No enforcement powers; (3) Political appointments — may not be independent; (4) State Women's Commissions: capacity varies hugely. CEDAW (Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women): India ratified 1993 with reservations; Article 12: States must ensure equality in healthcare (including MCH, family planning). CEDAW shadow reports: Women's groups submit parallel reports to CEDAW Committee — highlights India's gaps in reproductive health. HEO: women's health rights; CEDAW standards; NCW for escalation of reproductive health violations.

question: भारत में 'Health in the Constitution's Preamble' — Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity को health rights के साथ critically connect करें।

options.text: Preamble — legally enforceable provisions contain करता है

Preamble: Justice (social, economic, political) — health equity; Liberty — bodily autonomy, reproductive choice; Equality — anti-discrimination in healthcare (Art. 14/15); Fraternity — community solidarity in health (ASHA model, herd immunity). Preamble = interpretive aid for Art. 21 health rights; Kesavananda — Preamble = basic structure
Preamble — health को specifically mention करता है
Preamble — Fundamental Rights के under enforceable है court में

explanation: Constitutional Preamble and Health Rights: Preamble: 'We, the People of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic and to secure to all its citizens: Justice, social, economic and political; Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; Equality of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all Fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation.' Health connections: (1) Social Justice: health equity — poor, marginalized must access health; Art. 47 (nutrition, public health) = social justice DPSP; (2) Economic Justice: OOPE reduces economic justice; PM-JAY, free medicine = economic justice in health; (3) Liberty: bodily autonomy — right to refuse treatment; reproductive choices (Puttaswamy); (4) Equality: Art. 14 — no discrimination in healthcare; Art. 15(3): special provisions for women/children; (5) Fraternity: solidarity — herd immunity requires community vaccination; ASHA model = community caring for community; dignity = treating patients with respect. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Preamble = part of Constitution; reflects its basic structure. Preamble as interpretive tool: Courts use Preamble to interpret Fundamental Rights in broader context. Preamble not judicially enforceable per se. HEO: embodies all four values — just, equitable, dignified, community-oriented health promotion.

question: भारत में 'PM-JAY Governance Structure' को critically examine करें — National Health Authority, insurance vs. trust model, और accountability framework।

options.text: PM-JAY — एक traditional government health scheme है जो Ministry of Health directly implement करती है

PM-JAY: National Health Authority (NHA) = autonomous body under MoHFW; insurance vs. trust model (states choose); empanelled hospitals — quality standards; anti-fraud unit (₹491 crore fraud detected); state health agencies (SHA); PMJAY + state schemes convergence; 15.5 crore AB Health Account holders registered; financial sustainability concern
PM-JAY — केवल private hospitals में treatment देता है
NHA — Ministry of Finance के under है

explanation: PM-JAY Governance — Critical Analysis: Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) launched September 2018: ₹5 lakh/family/year for secondary and tertiary hospitalization; targeting 10.74 crore SECC-identified families. Institutional structure: (1) National Health Authority (NHA): autonomous body under MoHFW; CEO-led; policy + IT + anti-fraud; (2) State Health Agencies (SHA): state-level implementation; (3) Insurance mode: Centre + state share premium; commercial insurer (e.g., United India); (4) Trust mode: state government is insurer; pays claims directly; 9 states opted trust mode. Empanelment: Hospitals must meet NABH/LaQshya quality criteria; government + private; 25,000+ hospitals empanelled. Anti-fraud: NHA Anti-Fraud Unit; Artificial Intelligence surveillance (duplicate claims, high-value unusual procedures); ₹491 crore fraud detected 2019-2022. Integration with state schemes: 'Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY + State Schemes' — states add top-up; Tamil Nadu (Chief Minister's Comprehensive Health Insurance) combined. Financial sustainability: (1) Moral hazard — upcoding (billing higher category treatment than delivered); (2) Cream-skimming (easy cases empanelled); (3) Capitation vs. FFS tension; (4) Premium sufficiency — actuarial studies show underfunding. ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account): 15.5 crore+ registered for health record portability. HEO: beneficiary enrollment awareness; hospital empanelment assistance.

question: भारत में 'Social Determinants of Health' को constitutional provisions और governance में critically examine करें — Art. 15B, Housing, Sanitation, Clean Energy।

options.text: Social determinants of health — India के governance framework में absent हैं

WHO CSDH (2008): SDH = conditions in which people live; India's constitutional SDH provisions: Art. 47 (nutrition/water), Art. 21 (housing via Olga Tellis), Art. 39 (equitable resource distribution); housing (PMAY), sanitation (SBM), clean energy (PMUY), MGNREGS — all SDH policies with health implications; intersectoral action = HEO's mandate
Social determinants — Health Ministry alone can address
MGNREGS का health outcomes से कोई documented relationship नहीं है

explanation: Social Determinants of Health in Indian Governance: WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health (2008, Marmot report): 'The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age.' 10 SDH: Income, Education, Employment, Social exclusion, Working conditions, Food, Housing, Water, Health behaviors, Social support. Constitutional provisions for SDH: (1) Art. 47: nutrition, standard of living, public health — state responsibility; (2) Art. 21: Housing — Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985): right to livelihood including shelter; (3) Art. 39: equitable distribution of resources — land reform, food security; (4) Art. 42: maternity relief — working conditions. Governance programs addressing SDH: (1) PMAY (Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana) — housing → less crowding, better TB prevention; (2) SBM (Swachh Bharat Mission) — sanitation → diarrheal disease reduction; (3) PMUY (Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana) — clean cooking fuel → indoor air pollution reduction → maternal/child health; (4) MGNREGS — income → food, healthcare expenditure; evidence: states with higher MGNREGS spending show lower child malnutrition; (5) MDM (Mid-Day Meal) — school nutrition → enrollment; (6) NFSA — food security. Intersectoral action (ISA): Health in All Policies (HiAP) — HEO's mandate: coordinate with other departments for SDH. Marmot's 6 domains in Indian context: daily living conditions, power, money, resources.

question: भारत में 'Rajya Sabha की health legislation में role' को critically examine करें — health bills as Money Bills और federal character।

options.text: Rajya Sabha — health legislation में कोई role नहीं रखती

Rajya Sabha = Council of States; health bills pass through both Houses; Money Bill (Art. 110) — only Lok Sabha; NMC Act, MHA 2017, Transgender Act 2019 passed both houses; RPWD Act 2016 — Rajya Sabha recommended amendments incorporated; Rajya Sabha delay — NMC Bill stalled; federal character — state interests represented
All health legislation — Money Bills हैं इसलिए केवल Lok Sabha pass करती है
Rajya Sabha — health bills में amendments suggest नहीं कर सकती

explanation: Rajya Sabha and Health Legislation: Art. 79-122: Parliamentary structure. Rajya Sabha = Council of States (federal chamber); 245 members; not directly elected; state legislatures elect + Presidential nominees. Health bills process: (1) Ordinary Bills (Art. 107): introduced in either House; requires passage by both; Joint Sitting (Art. 108) in case of deadlock; (2) Money Bills (Art. 110): only introduced in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can recommend amendments but Lok Sabha can reject; if Rajya Sabha holds for 14 days → deemed passed. Health bills as Ordinary Bills: NMC Act 2020 — ordinary bill; passed both Houses; Rajya Sabha: NMC Bill debates — concerns raised about bridge course, autonomy; some amendments incorporated; Mental Healthcare Act 2017 — both Houses; Transgender Persons Act 2019 — both Houses (Rajya Sabha originally passed different version → reconciled). Health bills with financial components: PM-JAY appropriation = part of Finance Bill/Demands for Grants = Money Bill track. RPWD Act 2016: Rajya Sabha role — disability community lobbied RS members; RS recommended amendments on healthcare provisions. Rajya Sabha delay as accountability tool: Government sometimes faces RS scrutiny when lacking majority — health bill passage requires broader consensus. HEO relevance: parliamentary debate on health bills shapes programs HEO implements.

question: भारत में 'National AIDS Control Policy' की evolution को governance framework और civil society partnership के संदर्भ में critically analyze करें।

options.text: India में HIV/AIDS response — purely government-driven है, civil society की कोई role नहीं

NACP Phase I (1992) — III (2007-12) — IV (2012-17) — V (2021-26); India's HIV response: rights-based since Phase III; civil society central (Avahan, PLHIV networks); target populations (MSM, sex workers, PWID) — harm reduction; NACO under MoHFW; HIV AIDS Act 2017 — legislative backing; 2030 target: 95-95-95
NACO — autonomous body independent of Ministry of Health है
India का HIV burden — sub-Saharan Africa के समान है

explanation: National AIDS Control Policy Evolution: NACO (National AIDS Control Organisation) under MoHFW. NACP Phases: (1) Phase I (1992-99): Sentinel surveillance, blood safety, awareness; ₹84 crore World Bank; (2) Phase II (1999-2006): Prevention of parent to child transmission (PPTCT); VCTCs; (3) Phase III (2007-12): Rights-based approach; Key Populations (KP) programs (TG, sex workers, MSM, PWID); ₹2,500 crore; Target Setting using Modes of Transmission Study; Avahan (Bill Gates Foundation) — bridge populations; (4) Phase IV (2012-17): Consolidation; free ART scale-up (85 lakh+ on ART); free CD4 testing; (5) Phase V (2021-26): Ending AIDS as public health threat; 95-95-95 target (95% know status, 95% on treatment, 95% virally suppressed) by 2030. Civil Society Partnership: (1) Network of People Living with HIV India (NPHIV+); (2) India HIV/AIDS Alliance; (3) Avahan — largest private HIV prevention program; (4) Sex worker collectives (DMSC — Durbar Mahila Samanwaya Committee, Kolkata) — community-led HIV prevention. India's success: (1) HIV prevalence declined from 0.41% (2007) to 0.20% (2021); (2) New infections declining; (3) PPTCT: nearly 100% coverage. Challenges: Stigma, HIV AIDS Act 2017 implementation, KP programs political resistance in some states.

question: भारत में 'Immoral Traffic Prevention Act (ITPA) 1956' और sex workers' health rights को critically examine करें।

options.text: ITPA 1956 — sex workers को criminalize करता है directly

ITPA 1956: criminalizes brothel-keeping, soliciting, living on earnings of sex worker — NOT sex work itself; Supreme Court 2022 3-judge bench: sex workers = 'workers'; right to live with dignity; protection from violence; NACO programs: STI/HIV prevention for sex workers; criminalization → health risk (hurried transactions, no condom negotiation)
India में sex work — completely legal और regulated है
SC 2022 judgment — sex workers को voting rights नहीं देता

explanation: ITPA 1956 and Sex Workers' Health: Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956: Does NOT criminalize the act of sex work (individual selling sex) — criminalizes: (1) Brothel-keeping; (2) Soliciting in public places; (3) Pimping (living on earnings of sex worker); (4) Trafficking. SC Judgment May 2022 (X v. State of Maharashtra/Budhadev Karmaskar): 3-judge bench — sex workers are workers entitled to dignity; recommendations: (1) Sex workers not to be arrested for working; (2) Condoms cannot be treated as evidence of sex work; (3) Minors found with sex workers → not assumed to be sex workers; (4) Police must treat sex workers with dignity. NACO programs: 'Targeted Interventions (TI)': STI clinics for sex workers; condom promotion; peer educators (sex worker-to-sex worker). Health risks from criminalization: (1) Fear of police → hurried transactions → no condom negotiation → higher STI/HIV risk; (2) Cannot report violence (police will arrest); (3) Avoid health facilities (fear of exposure). International: UNAIDS, Amnesty International recommend decriminalization for public health outcomes — evidence from New Zealand. India: Partial decriminalization via SC 2022 guidelines. NACP Phase V: Community-led programs for sex workers — evidence-based. HEO: non-judgmental health services; STI/HIV prevention for sex workers.

question: भारत में 'Health Sector Performance-Based Financing (PBF)' को critically examine करें — JSY, NHM RoP, और incentive distortions।

options.text: Performance-based financing — India में health sector में नहीं है

India's PBF in health: JSY (cash incentive for institutional delivery); ASHA incentives (60+ tasks); RoP (Record of Proceedings) — NHM fund releases tied to state performance; VHSNC untied funds; BUT: perverse incentives — institutional delivery without quality = high; ASHA burnout; gaming of HMIS data; Goodhart's Law applies
PBF — World Bank द्वारा India में impose किया गया है
JSY cash incentives — maternal mortality reduction में कोई role नहीं था

explanation: Performance-Based Financing (PBF) in Indian Health: Definition: Linking payment/funding to measurable health outputs/outcomes. India's PBF models: (1) JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana): Cash transfer for institutional delivery — ₹1,400 rural poor woman + ASHA incentive. Result: Institutional delivery: 38.7% (2005-06) → 88.6% (NFHS-5 2019-21). But quality gap: 'obstetric transition' — facilities may not have required quality; (2) ASHA Incentives: 60+ tasks with specific incentive amounts; creates focus on incentivized tasks; non-incentivized tasks neglected (household visits, non-JSY MCH); (3) NHM Record of Proceedings (RoP): State PIPs approved; funds released in tranches based on utilization and targets; performance monitoring; (4) VHSNC Untied Funds (₹10,000/village): flexible, community-led allocation. Perverse incentives: (1) Goodhart's Law: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' — HMIS data inflated when tied to funding; (2) C-section rate explosion in empanelled hospitals (PM-JAY) — Caesarean = higher package rate; (3) ASHA burnout — multiple tasks, variable payments; (4) JSY targets → facility delivery without quality → maternal near-miss events in poor facilities. HEO: monitoring PBF outcomes; ensuring quality not just quantity; ASHA support for realistic task completion.

question: भारत में 'Judicial Activism vs. Judicial Restraint' को health policy में critically examine करें — resource allocation PIL और separation of powers।

options.text: Supreme Court — always health resource allocation में intervene करता है

Judicial Activism: Paschim Banga (1996) — emergency care obligation; PIL ordering hospital creation; Judicial Restraint: courts reluctant to order budget allocation (BALCO — state enterprise closures); health resource allocation = 'polycentric' issues; SC has tried to balance — setting minimum standards without dictating how; EWS reservation in medical education = judicial-legislative balance
Separation of powers — courts को health से completely exclude करता है
Courts — always defer to executive in health matters completely

explanation: Judicial Activism vs. Restraint in Health: Judicial Activism in health: (1) Paschim Banga (1996): emergency care = state obligation; (2) Murli Deora (2001): smoking ban in public places; (3) BALCO dissent (J. Kirpal): courts can issue directions even in policy matters if FRs involved; (4) Environmental PILs (MC Mehta): detailed implementation directions. Judicial Restraint: (1) Courts acknowledge limitation in resource-intensive orders; (2) BALCO v. Union of India (2002): policy decisions regarding economic enterprises = executive domain; (3) Budget allocation = Parliament's domain (separation of powers); (4) Comprehensive healthcare cannot be ordered by courts — 'polycentric' policy (Lon Fuller): many interconnected issues, no simple judicial solution. Balance: (1) Setting minimum standards: emergency care must be provided (Paschim Banga) — but court doesn't specify how; (2) Process review: was decision rational, fair? (Wednesbury unreasonableness); (3) EWS reservation in medical education (2019): SC upheld 10% EWS reservation in NEET — validates legislative health access policy. COVID vaccine mandate: Petitions challenging mandatory vaccination — HC: not strictly mandatory but 'strongly encouraged'; SC upheld government's vaccination policy — judicial deference to executive expert judgment. HEO: courts as backstop for health rights, not primary service delivery mechanism.

question: भारत में 'Zonal Councils और Inter-State Health Cooperation' को critically examine करें।

options.text: Zonal Councils — health matters directly coordinate करते हैं regularly

Zonal Councils (States Reorganisation Act 1956): 5 zones (Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western, Central); advisory — health cooperation = informal; no health-specific mandate; vector-borne disease cross-border (dengue, malaria) needs ISC/Zonal Council; vector control = state, surveillance = IDSP (Central); cross-border NHM referrals = ad hoc; need institutionalized health ISC
Zonal Councils — binding decisions issue करते हैं states को
IDSP — state boundaries के पार surveillance automatically coordinate करता है

explanation: Zonal Councils and Health Cooperation: Zonal Councils: Established under States Reorganisation Act 1956; 5 zones: Northern (J&K, HP, Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana, Delhi, Chandigarh), Southern (AP, Karnataka, Kerala, TN, Puducherry), Eastern (Assam, WB, Bihar, Odisha, Jharkhand, NE states), Western (Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, MP, Chhattisgarh), Central (UP, Uttarakhand). Composition: Home Minister (Centre, Chair) + CMs + 2 ministers from each state. Nature: Advisory; decisions not binding. Health in Zonal Councils: No specific health mandate; but cross-state health issues discussed informally; limited health agenda. Cross-border health challenges: (1) Vector-borne diseases: dengue, malaria, Aedes aegypti cross state borders — need coordinated vector control; (2) Outbreaks: cholera, COVID — state boundaries don't respect; (3) Health referrals: patients cross state borders for tertiary care — PMJAY portability helps; (4) Air quality: Delhi + NCR states (UP, Haryana) — GRAP requires coordination; Northern Zonal Council relevant. IDSP (Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme): Central system; state IDSP units; PHQ (Portal of Health Quality) — cross-state notification system exists but underused. Reform need: Health standing committee under relevant Zonal Council; or use ISC (Art. 263) for cross-state health issues. HEO: cross-state referral networks; disease surveillance data sharing.

question: भारत में 'NFSA 2013 Supreme Court orders' और 'Right to Food' enforcement को critically examine करें — PUCL v. Union of India।

options.text: Supreme Court — food rights में intervene नहीं करती

PUCL v. Union of India (2001-ongoing): SC — right to food = Art. 21; 'Commissioners' appointed for monitoring; ICDS universalization, MDM in schools — SC orders; grain rotting in FCI godowns vs. starvation deaths = constitutional violation; NFSA 2013 partially codified SC orders; food = health connection direct
PUCL case — केवल PDS को address करता है
SC appointed Food Commissioners — binding orders नहीं दे सकते

explanation: Right to Food and PUCL Case: People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) v. Union of India (2001): PIL on starvation deaths in Rajasthan despite overflowing FCI (Food Corporation of India) grain godowns. SC intervention: (1) Right to food = Art. 21 (right to life); (2) Appointed two Food Commissioners (Harsh Mander and N.C. Saxena); (3) Series of interim orders: ICDS to be universalized in all habitations; Midday Meal Scheme — cooked meals in all primary schools; PDS — grain to be provided to all BPL; Antodaya Anna Yojana — poorest of poor; (4) States to submit compliance reports. NFSA 2013: Partially codified SC orders — statutory basis for what was judicial order.
